title: Read the gross-to-net revenue bridge every month, not net revenue alone
hypothesis: If we track gross revenue, discounts, refunds, chargebacks and shipping collected as separate lines every month, then a revenue change gets the right cause because net revenue alone hides which of the 4 levers moved.

signal.check: The monthly report shows only net revenue or bank deposits, with no line for gross revenue, discounts, refunds or shipping collected.

expected_effect.size: in the source example net revenue rose 100k to 110k while gross stayed near 120k both months; the real story was falling refunds

risk.note: This is a reporting change. Nothing on the live store changes.

prerequisites: Gross revenue, discounts, refunds, chargebacks and shipping collected by day from the store platform
steps: Pull gross revenue, discounts, refunds, chargebacks and shipping collected by day from the store platform, not the accounting system alone.
Build net revenue as gross minus discounts minus refunds minus chargebacks plus shipping collected.
Add all 4 bridge lines to the monthly report next to net revenue.
When net revenue moves, check which of the 4 lines caused it before drawing a conclusion.

test.method: Compare a month where net revenue rose against the 4 bridge lines to confirm which one explains the rise.
test.measure: gross revenue, discounts, refunds, chargebacks, shipping collected, net revenue

title: Exclude sales tax, VAT or GST from revenue before computing any margin
hypothesis: If we strip pass-through sales tax, VAT or GST out of revenue before computing margin, then the margin percent is not inflated or deflated by a number the store never keeps.

signal.check: A margin calculation or dashboard uses a revenue figure that still includes tax collected at checkout.

expected_effect.size: removing a 9 percent tax line from a 100 dollar order changed the reported margin from 24 percent to 26.4 percent in the source's t-shirt example

risk.note: Pure reporting correction with no operational change.

prerequisites: Sales tax or GST collected reported as its own line, separate from list price
steps: Confirm whether the store's reported revenue figure includes tax collected at checkout.
Subtract tax, VAT or GST collected from gross revenue before any further margin math.
Recompute every downstream margin (CM1, CM2, CM3) off the tax-excluded revenue.
Note the correction in the report so the new percent is not read as a real change.

test.method: Recompute last month's margin with and without tax excluded and compare the two percentages.
test.read_point: Once, then keep tax excluded going forward

title: Treat refunds, discounts and shipping collected as profit levers to test, not fixed facts
hypothesis: If we test lowering refunds, cutting discount overuse and raising shipping charges, then net revenue rises with no extra traffic because these 3 lines are levers, not fixed costs.
does_not_apply_when: Refunds and discounts already sit under 5 percent of gross revenue

signal.check: Refunds plus discounts exceed 5 percent of gross revenue, or the store has never tested a shipping charge.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source says most brands under-collect shipping

risk.note: Raising a shipping charge can hurt conversion; test it as an offer change first.

prerequisites: Refund rate and discount rate by category
A landing page or checkout test tool for shipping price
steps: Compute refunds and discounts as a percent of gross revenue for the last 3 months.
If either exceeds 5 percent, find the top cause (product, category, discount code).
Hand a shipping charge change to the conversion rate optimization track as an A/B test, not a blanket change.
Track net shipping cost (shipping collected minus outbound shipping cost) monthly.

test.method: A/B test a shipping charge or a reduced discount code and measure conversion rate alongside net revenue.
test.read_point: After the test reaches a decision-grade sample, per 09-CRO

title: Label every margin figure as CM1, CM2 or CM3 so nobody guesses its scope
hypothesis: If every margin number in a report or formula carries its CM1, CM2 or CM3 label, then the team stops setting budgets off the wrong margin because the scope is unmistakable.

signal.check: A report or a person says "gross margin" or "contribution margin" with no stated scope.

expected_effect.size: unknown; both source presenters warn the same word is used 3 different ways in their own material

prerequisites: CM1, CM2 and CM3 already defined and computed for the store
steps: Define CM1 (product margin), CM2 (after cost of delivery) and CM3 (after variable marketing) once in a shared doc.
Add the CM label to every dashboard, spreadsheet and report cell that shows a margin.
Reject any number in a meeting called just "margin" until its scope is named.
Re-check the labels every time a new report or dashboard is built.

test.method: Spot-check 5 reports for unlabeled margin numbers after the rule is adopted.

title: Never set a marketing budget or CAC target off product margin (CM1)
hypothesis: If we set the CAC ceiling off CM2 (after cost of delivery) instead of CM1 (product margin only), then the budget stops assuming a margin that is not really there.

signal.check: The team quotes a margin like 70 percent to justify ad spend, but that number has not been checked against fulfillment, fees, freight and returns.

expected_effect.size: source example: 70 percent product margin became 24 percent true gross margin once shipping, pick and pack, fees, freight and a refund allowance were subtracted

risk.note: Reversible on paper, but a budget already spent against the wrong margin is real cash lost.

prerequisites: A completed CM2 build for at least the top SKU (see the landed cost and cost of delivery ideas)
steps: Find every margin number currently used to justify ad spend or set CPA targets.
Check whether that number already subtracts fulfillment, fees, freight and a refund and discount allowance.
If not, recompute it as CM2 before using it for any budget decision.
Reset the CAC target and any live campaign target off the corrected CM2.

test.method: Compare the CAC target implied by the old margin figure against the CAC ceiling implied by CM2.

title: Set the CAC ceiling at CM2 per new order, not a round number
hypothesis: If we compute CM2 per new order and use it as the hard CAC ceiling, then acquisition spend stops going past the point where a new customer's first order loses money.
does_not_apply_when: A cohort with 6 or more months of history proves the tail repays a higher CAC

signal.check: There is no written CAC ceiling, or the ceiling was picked by feel rather than from CM2 per new order.

expected_effect.size: the ceiling equals CM2 dollars per new order, for example a source case where CAC needed to stay at or under 83 dollars

risk.note: Lowering a live CAC target can cut volume; pair with the media buyer before changing bids.

prerequisites: CM2 per new order computed (aov_new minus product cogs minus fulfillment)
steps: Compute aov_new and CM2 per new order for the current month.
Set breakeven_cac equal to CM2 per new order.
Subtract the required OPEX and profit contribution per order to get the operating CAC ceiling.
Share the ceiling with whoever runs media so bids and budgets respect it.

test.method: Track cac_media against the ceiling weekly and flag any week it crosses above.

title: Track contribution after marketing (CM3) as the core monthly profitability gauge
hypothesis: If we report CM3 (net revenue minus cost of delivery minus variable marketing) every month, then a business that looks fine on revenue but is losing money after marketing gets caught before OPEX makes it worse.

signal.check: No single number in the monthly report answers whether the business made money after marketing, before OPEX.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source states nothing below CM3 fixes a business that is not CM3 positive

risk.note: Reporting addition; no operational change by itself.

prerequisites: CM2 and variable marketing spend known for the period
steps: Compute cm3_media (CM2 minus ad spend) daily and cm3_loaded (CM2 minus all variable marketing) monthly.
Put CM3 at the top of the monthly report, above revenue growth.
Flag any month where CM3 is negative before discussing OPEX or hiring.
Trace a negative CM3 to marketing spend or cost of delivery using the fault rule.

test.method: Compare months where CM3 is positive vs negative against the store's own cash position.

title: Compute unit economics per basket, not per unit, and say which count is used
hypothesis: If we compute CAC, CM2 and margin per order (basket) instead of per unit, then the numbers stop overstating fulfillment cost per item and understating CAC per order.

signal.check: A margin or CAC figure is computed per unit sold rather than per order, and the store's basket carries more than 1 item on average.

expected_effect.size: DTC baskets run 1.1 to 1.7 units per order in the sources

prerequisites: Units per order tracked alongside orders
steps: Compute units_per_order = total units / total orders for the period.
Rebuild CM2, CAC ceiling and any per-item cost figure on a per-order basis.
Label every metric with whether it is per order, per unit or per customer.
Reject any new report that mixes the 3 counts without saying which one it uses.

test.method: Recompute CM2 per unit and per order side by side and check how far apart they are.
test.read_point: Once at setup, then whenever units per order shifts materially

title: Audit small per-order fulfillment costs once the store has real order volume
hypothesis: If we divide each fulfillment line (freight, pick and pack, fees) by revenue monthly, then a small per-order cost that moved gets caught before it erases profit at volume.
does_not_apply_when: The store ships well under 50 orders a month, where the lever sits elsewhere

signal.check: Fulfillment cost lines (freight, pick and pack, packaging, fees) are not tracked as a percent of revenue month to month.

expected_effect.size: source claims a couple of dollars per order across thousands of orders is the difference between tens of thousands of dollars of profit or loss

risk.note: Monitoring step; any fix that follows is a separate decision.

prerequisites: Fulfillment cost lines broken out: pick and pack, packing materials, outbound shipping, storage, fees
steps: List every fulfillment cost line separately: pick and pack, packing materials, outbound shipping, storage, warehouse staff, payment fee, marketplace fee.
Divide each line by net revenue for the month.
Compare each line's percent to the last 3 months to see which one moved.
Investigate and fix the line that moved before it compounds across more orders.

test.method: Track each fulfillment line as a percent of revenue for 3 consecutive months.

title: Watch gross margin percent, not gross profit dollars, around a promo month
hypothesis: If we read gross margin percent instead of raw profit dollars during and after a promo, then a dip explained by the discount reads as fine while a dip from cost lines gets caught.

signal.check: A promo month's margin dip has not been broken down into the discount effect vs a cost-line effect (freight, pick and pack).

expected_effect.size: source example: orders nearly doubled in a sale month, margin percent fell from the discount, then recovered the next month

prerequisites: Monthly gross margin percent and discount rate by month
steps: Compute gross margin percent for the promo month and the 2 months before and after.
Compute what the discount alone should explain, using the discount rate.
Check whether the remaining dip, if any, comes from cost lines like air freight or higher pick and pack.
Flag only the unexplained portion as a real problem.

test.method: Compare the modeled discount-only margin dip against the actual margin dip for the promo month.

title: Track sales tax or GST nexus and registration thresholds in every market the store sells into
hypothesis: If we track nexus thresholds and marketplace-facilitator remittance rules by state or country, then the store registers and remits before a threshold is crossed instead of after an audit finds it.
does_not_apply_when: The store sells into only 1 tax jurisdiction

signal.check: The store sells into multiple states or countries with no written list of nexus thresholds or registration status per market.

expected_effect.size: unknown

risk.note: Missing this can create back tax and penalty exposure; verify against local rules before acting.

prerequisites: List of states or countries the store ships to
An accountant familiar with the relevant jurisdictions
steps: List every state or country the store has shipped meaningful volume into in the last 12 months.
For each, look up the nexus and registration threshold with the accountant or a web check.
Note which marketplaces already remit tax on the store's behalf (marketplace-facilitator rules).
Register in any market where the threshold has been crossed and none exists yet.

test.method: Review sales by state or country against nexus thresholds quarterly.

title: Book gift cards issued as a liability and recognize revenue only on redemption
hypothesis: If we book gift cards issued as deferred revenue and recognize revenue only when redeemed, then the P&L stops overstating revenue in the month a card is sold.
does_not_apply_when: The store does not sell gift cards

signal.check: Gift card sales are recorded as revenue at the time of sale instead of as a liability until redeemed.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects the timing of when gift card revenue is recognized

risk.note: Accounting correction; confirm the exact treatment with the accountant.

prerequisites: Gift card issuance and redemption data by date
steps: Set up a deferred-revenue liability account for gift cards issued.
Move the sale amount to revenue only when the card is redeemed against an order.
Estimate breakage (cards that never get redeemed) from redemption history and confirm the accounting treatment with the accountant.
Report outstanding gift card liability alongside cash and inventory.

test.method: Compare revenue recognized under the new method against the prior method for one quarter.

title: Build 1 documented landed cost per SKU using the backup test for every cost line
hypothesis: If we compute landed cost per SKU as purchase price plus inbound freight share plus duty share plus product packaging, checked with the backup test, then every margin built on top of it stops being wrong.

signal.check: COGS per SKU is a rough estimate, a blended average, or the supplier price alone, with no documented freight and duty allocation.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects an understated COGS figure to its true value

risk.note: Costing correction; does not touch live operations.

prerequisites: Purchase order records
Supplier, freight and duty invoices
An agreed allocation basis (weight, volume, value or units)
steps: For each SKU, gather purchase price net of supplier discounts and credits.
Add the freight share and duty share for that SKU's shipment, using 1 documented allocation basis.
Add product packaging cost (the retail box, not the shipping carton).
Apply the backup test to every line: would you have paid this cost if you had not bought these goods? Yes means COGS.
Record the landed cost with an effective date and recalculate when supplier price, exchange rate or freight changes.

test.method: Compare the new landed cost per SKU against the old blended or supplier-only cost.
test.read_point: Once per shipment, and whenever price, FX or freight changes

title: Keep 2 cost views side by side: statutory COGS and internal cost of delivery
hypothesis: If we keep statutory COGS and internal cost of delivery as 2 clearly labeled views instead of 1 mixed table, then the marketing decision uses the right margin and the statutory books stay compliant.

signal.check: There is only 1 COGS or margin table used for both the accountant's books and the marketing CAC decision.

expected_effect.size: unknown

risk.note: Structural change to reporting, not to operations.

prerequisites: A written accounting policy for statutory COGS scope
steps: Build the statutory COGS view per the accountant's written policy: purchase price, inbound freight, duty, product packaging.
Build the internal cost of delivery view: statutory COGS plus outbound shipping, pick and pack, storage, warehouse staff, payment and marketplace fees.
Label every table with which view it is.
Use internal COD for CM2 and the CAC ceiling; use statutory COGS for the compliance books.

test.method: Check that no report mixes the 2 views without a stated bridge between them.

title: Split product cost from fulfillment cost on the internal P&L instead of 1 COGS line
hypothesis: If we split product cost (manufacturing, import freight, duty, packaging) from fulfillment cost (pick and pack, 3PL, shipping, fees) on the internal P&L, then whichever cost moved becomes visible instead of hidden inside 1 line.

signal.check: The internal P&L has a single COGS line covering both product cost and fulfillment cost.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Landed cost per SKU
Fulfillment cost per order breakdown
steps: Separate the internal P&L COGS line into product cost and fulfillment cost.
Track each as a percent of revenue every month.
Compare month over month to see which one is trending the wrong way.
Route any fix to the right owner: sourcing for product cost, ops for fulfillment cost.

test.method: Track both lines as a percent of revenue for 3 months and compare trend direction.

title: Land freight and duty per unit per shipment using 1 documented allocation basis
hypothesis: If we attach every freight and duty invoice to its purchase order and allocate it across SKUs by 1 documented basis, then landed cost stops being a guess and stays consistent shipment to shipment.

signal.check: Freight and duty invoices arrive and sit unmatched to a purchase order, or the allocation basis changes shipment to shipment.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects an unallocated or inconsistently allocated freight and duty cost

risk.note: Process fix; no live operational risk.

prerequisites: Purchase orders with SKU-level unit counts
Freight and duty invoices
steps: Pick 1 allocation basis for every shipment: weight, volume, value or units.
When a freight or duty invoice arrives, link it to its purchase order the same day.
Allocate the shipment total across the SKUs in it using the chosen basis.
Recalculate landed cost whenever supplier price, exchange rate or freight changes, and version the table with an effective date.

test.method: Check that allocated freight and duty across the last 3 shipments sum to the invoice totals and use the same basis.

title: Split product packaging (COGS) from shipping packaging (fulfillment expense)
hypothesis: If we split the retail box (product packaging, COGS) from the shipping carton (fulfillment expense) on mixed packaging invoices, then landed cost and fulfillment cost each carry the right amount.

signal.check: A packaging invoice covers both the retail box and the shipping carton and is coded to 1 account.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Packaging invoices itemized by line, or a way to split them
steps: Review the last 3 packaging invoices for mixed retail box and shipping carton charges.
Split each invoice line into product packaging (COGS) and shipping packaging (fulfillment expense).
Update the chart of accounts mapping so future invoices split automatically where possible.
Add the corrected product packaging cost into the landed cost table.

test.method: Confirm the next 3 packaging invoices are split correctly at posting time.

title: Always include outbound shipping in the internal cost of delivery view
hypothesis: If outbound shipping to the customer always sits inside the internal cost of delivery, no matter its statutory treatment, then the CAC ceiling is never set off a margin that ignores a real per-order cost.

signal.check: CM2 or the CAC ceiling is computed without subtracting outbound shipping cost.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects CM2 downward by the true outbound shipping cost per order

prerequisites: Outbound shipping cost per order from the 3PL or carrier invoices
steps: Confirm the outbound shipping cost per order is captured, not just shipping revenue collected.
Add it to the internal cost of delivery formula regardless of the statutory policy.
Recompute CM2 and the CAC ceiling with this line included.
Keep the statutory books following the written policy separately, per the dual cost view.

test.method: Recompute CM2 with and without outbound shipping to see the gap.
test.read_point: Once at setup, then part of every CM2 build

title: Put payment and marketplace fees in cost of delivery for the internal view, never OPEX
hypothesis: If payment gateway and marketplace fees sit inside internal cost of delivery instead of OPEX, then CM2 correctly reflects that these fees vary with revenue.

signal.check: Payment or marketplace fees are booked into OPEX or a general expense line instead of cost of delivery.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects CM2 by moving a variable cost out of the fixed OPEX bucket

prerequisites: Payment gateway and marketplace fee rates by channel
steps: Find where payment and marketplace fees currently sit in the chart of accounts.
Move them into the internal cost of delivery bucket if they are in OPEX.
Recompute the 4-bucket P&L shares after the move.
Keep the statutory view following the accountant's written policy.

test.method: Check that OPEX percent falls and cost of delivery percent rises by the same amount after the reclass.
test.read_point: Next monthly close after the reclass

title: Reclassify warehouse staff cost into cost of delivery at cost per package shipped
hypothesis: If we move warehouse staff cost into cost of delivery at daily cost divided by packages shipped per day, then gross margin stops being overstated by staff cost hiding in OPEX.

signal.check: Warehouse or fulfilment staff who pick, pack and ship orders are booked entirely in OPEX with no per-order cost computed.

expected_effect.size: source example: 400 dollars a day divided by 100 packages equals 4 dollars an order added to cost of delivery

risk.note: Statutory P&L can stay unchanged if the accountant does not agree; apply in the internal view only.

prerequisites: Daily cost of fulfillment staff
Packages shipped per day
Accounting system tracking categories set up
steps: Compute the daily cost of staff who pick, pack and ship orders.
Divide by packages shipped per day to get a per-order cost.
Tag those staff in the accounting system and build a custom internal P&L that moves them into cost of delivery.
Add the per-order figure into the fulfillment cost formula.

test.method: Check that OPEX falls and cost of delivery rises by the same dollar amount, and CM2 percent falls accordingly.
test.read_point: Next monthly close after the reclass

title: Apply churn only to subscriptions, and always state the period it is measured over
hypothesis: If churn is computed only for subscription customers, with the period always stated (monthly vs annual), then a one-off store stops asking for a churn number that does not apply to it, and a subscription store stops confusing 11 percent monthly with 11 percent annual.
does_not_apply_when: The store has no subscription product

signal.check: A churn figure is being requested or reported for a non-subscription store, or a churn rate appears with no stated period.

expected_effect.size: source example: 11 percent monthly and 11 percent annual are very different figures

prerequisites: Subscriber counts by period
steps: Confirm the store has an actual subscription product before computing churn.
For a non-subscription store, use cohort retention instead of churn.
State the period (monthly or annual) every time a churn figure is reported.
Reject any churn figure in a report with no stated period.

test.method: Audit the last 3 reports mentioning churn for a stated period.

title: Compute churn against the prior period's subscriber base, never the current total or new signups
hypothesis: If churn always divides cancellations by the prior period's subscriber base, then adding a strong month of new signups does not accidentally make the churn rate look better than it is.

signal.check: Churn is computed by dividing cancellations by the current period's total subscribers or by new signups instead of the prior period's base.

expected_effect.size: source example: 100 prior subscribers plus 50 new minus 9 cancelled gives 9 percent churn against the prior base, not 6 percent against the new total

prerequisites: Subscriber counts by period: prior base, new, cancellations
steps: Pull the prior period's ending subscriber count.
Divide the period's cancellations by that prior-period base, not the current total.
Recompute any historical churn figures that used the wrong denominator.
Document the correct formula so future reports use it consistently.

test.method: Recompute churn for the last 3 months with both denominators and compare.
test.read_point: Once at correction, then every churn report

title: Use average lifetime (1 divided by churn) only as a fallback, and be conservative on the churn assumption
hypothesis: If average lifetime is used only as a quick fallback with a conservative churn assumption, and replaced with cohort data as soon as it exists, then early LTV estimates do not overstate a new subscription business's real customer value.
does_not_apply_when: A cohort table with enough history already exists

signal.check: Average lifetime (1 / churn) is being used as the ongoing LTV method for a subscription business that already has 6 or more months of cohort data.

expected_effect.size: bands in the source: 25 percent churn equals 4 months lifetime; 20 percent equals 5; 15 percent equals 6.7; 10 percent equals 10; 5 percent equals 20

prerequisites: A churn rate assumption, even a conservative placeholder
steps: For a new subscription business with little data, use a conservative churn assumption (the source uses 25 percent monthly for a subscription box model).
Compute average lifetime as 1 divided by churn, and use the survival-based annual-to-monthly conversion rather than the simple division.
Replace this fallback with the cohort-based method as soon as 6 or more months of real data exist.
Flag any LTV built on the fallback method as provisional in reports.

test.method: Compare the fallback LTV estimate against the cohort-based LTV once enough history accumulates.
test.read_point: Once 6 months of cohort data exist

title: Build separate unit economics for transactional and subscription customers
hypothesis: If transactional and subscription customers get separate unit economics instead of 1 blended view, then a rising subscription mix does not read as a mysterious margin decline when it is actually a shift toward lower-AOV, higher-lifetime customers.

signal.check: The store reports 1 blended CM percent with no split between transactional and subscription customers.

expected_effect.size: source claims subscribers carry lower AOV and margin per order but 3 to 5 times revenue per customer over time

prerequisites: Orders tagged as transactional or subscription
steps: Tag every order as transactional or subscription.
Compute AOV, CM2 and lifetime value separately for each group.
Expect blended CM percent to fall as subscription mix rises, and explain it with the split, not treat it as a mystery.
Report both segments side by side in the monthly ladder.

test.method: Track blended CM percent against subscription mix share for 2 quarters and confirm the split explains the trend.

title: Forecast transactional repeat orders with a rolling 6-month return rate
hypothesis: If transactional (non-subscription) repeat orders are forecast from a rolling 6-month return rate instead of a churn model, then the forecast fits how these customers actually behave, buying again every few months rather than canceling.
does_not_apply_when: The customer base is fully subscription-based

signal.check: Transactional repeat revenue is forecast with a churn-style model instead of a rolling 6-month return rate.

expected_effect.size: source experience: 3 to 5 percent of trailing-6-month customers reorder per month

prerequisites: Order history with customer id and order date for the trailing 6 months
steps: Compute the trailing 6-month customer count each month.
Apply the return rate (starting at 3 to 5 percent as a placeholder) to that trailing base.
Update the return rate assumption as the store's own history accumulates.
Use this instead of a churn or subscription model for non-subscription repeat forecasting.

test.method: Compare the rolling-rate forecast against actual transactional repeat orders for the next 2 months.

title: Treat vendor subscription claims as hypotheses to test, never as fact
hypothesis: If claims from subscription software vendors (default-to-subscription lifts, prepaid LTV gains, roll-off rates) are tested on the store's own data instead of cited as fact, then the store does not build a forecast or a cart flow on an unproven vendor number.

signal.check: A subscription forecast or cart design decision cites a vendor claim (like a specific signup lift percent) with no test run on the store's own traffic.

expected_effect.size: unknown, vendor claims in the source come with no sample size

risk.note: Default-to-subscription cart changes carry consent and negative-option billing risk; verify against the brand's auto-renewal consent rules before testing.

prerequisites: A way to A/B test cart or offer changes
steps: Flag any vendor-sourced number (signup lift, prepaid LTV gain, roll-off rate) used in a forecast or design decision.
Design a test on the store's own traffic before relying on the claim.
For any default-to-subscription cart test, check auto-renewal consent rules in the brand's market first.
Replace the vendor number with the store's own measured result once the test completes.

test.method: A/B test the specific vendor-claimed mechanic (for example, default-to-subscription vs opt-in) on the store's own checkout.
test.read_point: After the test reaches a decision-grade sample

title: Judge prepaid subscription plans on lifetime gross profit and cash timing, not per-order margin
hypothesis: If prepaid subscription plans are judged on lifetime gross profit and cash timing instead of per-order margin, then a prepaid discount that looks thin per order can still be the right offer because of the lifetime value and upfront cash it brings.

signal.check: A prepaid plan's discount is being evaluated only on its per-order margin, with no lifetime GP or cash-timing comparison against a one-time purchase.

expected_effect.size: source example: one-time LTV 54 dollars vs 146 at a 3-order prepaid and 198 at a 6-order prepaid; a small mix shift lifts weighted LTV 30 percent

risk.note: Modeling exercise; model with the brand's own retention data, not the vendor's.

prerequisites: The brand's own prepaid retention data, or a conservative placeholder
steps: Compute lifetime GP for a one-time purchase, a shorter prepaid plan and a longer prepaid plan.
Model with the brand's own retention data where available.
Compare the cash timing benefit (upfront payment) against the per-order margin given up.
Approve the prepaid structure that maximizes weighted lifetime GP across the expected mix, not the one with the best per-order margin.

test.method: Track actual lifetime GP for prepaid customers against the modeled figure after 1 full prepaid term.
test.read_point: After the first prepaid term completes

title: Size a subscription launch raise to the lowest cash month, not to the P&L break-even point
hypothesis: If a subscription launch's fundraise is sized to the lowest projected cash month instead of the P&L break-even month, then the business does not run out of cash months before the P&L says it should be fine.

signal.check: A subscription launch's raise amount was sized to reach P&L break-even, with no separate lowest-cash-month calculation.

expected_effect.size: source example: post-advertising CM covered nothing until month 11, payroll only from month 14 to 15; a 500,000 dollar raise was not enough, about 1.5 million was needed

risk.note: Under-raising for a subscription launch risks running out of cash mid-ramp.

prerequisites: A full monthly cash model for the launch, not just a P&L projection
steps: Build a monthly cash model for the launch, including when CM actually starts covering payroll.
Find the lowest projected cash month across the launch ramp.
Size the raise or facility to that lowest point plus a buffer, not to the P&L break-even month.
Re-check the model monthly against actuals during the ramp.

test.method: Track actual cash balance against the modeled lowest-cash-month projection during the launch ramp.

title: Test whether a conversion-lifting change actually lowers CAC before crediting it
hypothesis: If a landing page, offer or discount change that is expected to lift conversion is tested for its real effect on CAC, then a claimed CAC improvement is confirmed instead of assumed from a conversion-rate model alone.

signal.check: A change expected to raise conversion rate is credited with lowering CAC with no test confirming the actual CAC change.

expected_effect.size: unknown, CAC is a function of conversion rate; the size of the effect depends on the specific change tested

risk.note: Test design step; hand the actual test to the conversion rate optimization process.

prerequisites: Ability to run an A/B or staged test on the change
steps: Identify the specific change expected to raise conversion (offer, price, page element).
Design a test that measures both conversion rate and resulting CAC, not conversion rate alone.
Add back any discount cost into the CAC comparison per the discount-and-CAC pool rule.
Only credit the change with a CAC improvement once the test confirms it.

test.method: Run the A/B test to a decision-grade sample and compare CAC in both arms.
test.read_point: After the test reaches its pre-registered stopping point

title: Use a placeholder CAC for a new category launch, then replace it with observed CAC and re-forecast
hypothesis: If a new-category launch uses a clearly marked placeholder CAC with wide error bars, replaced by observed CAC as soon as real spend data exists, then the launch plan does not pretend to know a number nobody can know before launch.
does_not_apply_when: The product is in an existing category with known CAC history

signal.check: A new-category launch plan uses a single-point CAC assumption with no error bars and no plan to replace it once real data exists.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: A small-batch or early test spend to generate the first real CAC data point
steps: Mark the pre-launch CAC assumption clearly as a placeholder with a wide range, not a point estimate.
Launch a small test to generate the first real CAC observation.
Replace the placeholder with the observed CAC as soon as it exists.
Re-forecast the launch plan with the observed figure instead of the placeholder.

test.method: Compare the placeholder CAC range against the actual observed CAC after the first test batch.
test.read_point: As soon as the first real spend data exists

title: Build every startup or investor cash model with ad spend as the single lever driving new customers
hypothesis: If a startup or investor model treats ad spend as the single lever from which new customers, revenue, burn and runway all flow, then the model stays internally consistent instead of having spend, revenue and runway modeled as unrelated assumptions.
does_not_apply_when: The model is for an established brand with mature multi-channel acquisition

signal.check: A startup or raise model shows revenue, spend and runway as separately typed assumptions with no formula linking new customers to spend divided by CAC.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects an internally inconsistent model

prerequisites: A CAC assumption and a target ad spend schedule
steps: Set new_customers[month] = ad_spend[month] divided by CAC[month] as the model's core formula.
Keep all inputs in 1 place, formulas in a separate section, over a 48-month monthly horizon for an investor model.
Add a catch-all OPEX line, conservatively sized (about 10 percent of revenue as a starting placeholder).
Use conservative churn and lifetime-order assumptions, treating any upside as a bonus, not the base case.

test.method: Check that changing the ad spend assumption automatically flows through to new customers, revenue and runway in the model.
test.read_point: At model build, then whenever spend assumptions change

title: Do not plan on paid-media efficiency past the point where diminishing returns are expected to set in
hypothesis: If a growth plan flags the spend or revenue level where performance media typically hits diminishing returns and needs its own brand budget line, then the plan does not assume paid efficiency holds forever as spend grows.

signal.check: A growth plan assumes flat marketing efficiency well past a scale where the source flags returns typically diminish (about 30,000 to 40,000 dollars a day, or 20 to 30 million dollars in revenue).

expected_effect.size: flagged threshold is opinion and anecdote from 1 source, with no quantified budget size behind it; treat as a planning flag, not a hard number

risk.note: Planning flag only; this threshold is unverified and should be checked against the brand's own spend-efficiency curve.

prerequisites: The brand's own spend-vs-aMER curve
steps: Check the brand's own spend-vs-aMER curve for signs of flattening efficiency at current or planned spend levels.
Do not assume the source's 30,000 to 40,000 dollar daily spend threshold applies without checking the brand's own curve.
Flag the point where a brand budget line (beyond direct-response media) may be needed.
Revisit the flag as spend grows and the curve updates.

test.method: Track the brand's own fitted aMER curve for flattening as spend increases over several quarters.

title: Check all 4 hidden cash traps whenever profit and cash disagree
hypothesis: If every month where profit and cash disagree is checked against the 4 known traps (inventory bought in chunks, capitalized build cost, loan principal, tax accrued but paid in lumps), then the real cause is found instead of guessed at.

signal.check: A month shows profit and cash moving in different directions, with no systematic check against the 4 known causes.

expected_effect.size: unknown, names the cause of a profit-cash mismatch that a profitable store is usually already experiencing

prerequisites: Inventory purchase schedule
Capitalized asset and depreciation schedule
Loan schedule
Tax accrual and payment calendar
steps: Check whether inventory was bought in a large chunk this month but expensed only as it sells.
Check whether a capitalized build cost is being depreciated over time instead of hitting cash in 1 month.
Check whether loan principal repayment (which does not appear on the P&L) hit cash this month.
Check whether tax was accrued monthly but paid in a lump this month.
Name which of the 4 explains the gap before concluding anything else is wrong.

test.method: Apply the checklist to the next month where profit and cash disagree and confirm 1 of the 4 explains it.
test.read_point: Every month profit and cash disagree

title: Test CAC and churn sensitivity on every financial model before relying on it
hypothesis: If every model is tested for what CAC breaks even at different months and what churn level halves LTV, then a plan is not built on a single fragile assumption that a small miss could invalidate.

signal.check: A financial model or forecast is presented with a single CAC and churn assumption and no sensitivity range shown.

expected_effect.size: source example: 125 dollars breaks even by month 5, 225 dollars by month 11 in the same model

prerequisites: The base model already built
steps: Re-run the model at CAC plus and minus 25 percent to see the break-even shift.
Re-run the model at churn plus 5 points to see the LTV shift.
Present the sensitivity range alongside the base case in every plan or scenario answer.
Flag any plan that only holds together under the single-point assumption.

test.method: Check that the next 3 models presented include a CAC and churn sensitivity range.

title: When the ad account looks healthy but the business is not, check measurement, margin or cash
hypothesis: If a healthy-looking ad account paired with a business that is not improving triggers a check of measurement, margin and cash flow instead of more ad tweaks, then the real problem gets found instead of endless campaign optimization.

signal.check: Ad account metrics (ROAS, CPA) look fine or improving, but overall business profit or cash is not improving, and the team keeps optimizing campaigns anyway.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Monthly P&L and cash forecast alongside ad account metrics
steps: Confirm the ad account metrics look healthy or improving for the period.
Check whether the business's P&L or cash position actually improved in the same period.
If not, check measurement first (reconciliation gaps, attribution overlap).
Then check margin (COD, CM2) and cash flow (inventory, CCC) before touching campaigns further.

test.method: Run the monthly reconciliation and CM2 checks whenever ad metrics and business results diverge.
test.read_point: Every month ad metrics and business results diverge

title: Run a holdout test before pausing or cutting an ad that appears to sell itself
hypothesis: If a holdout test confirms whether a low-CPA or seemingly self-selling product's ads are actually driving incremental sales, then a pause decision is based on real incrementality instead of the one-line rule to never turn off an ad or the opposite instinct to cut anything with a high CPA.

signal.check: A decision to pause or keep running an ad on a product that sells at a low CPA or seems to sell without ads has been made with no holdout test.

expected_effect.size: unknown, the holdout determines whether the spend was incremental or wasted

risk.note: A holdout test temporarily reduces or removes spend on the tested product.

prerequisites: Enough baseline sales volume on the product to detect a holdout effect
steps: Identify a product or ad set where the ignore-the-one-liner rule applies: it may stock out soon, sit below the marginal-return frontier, or seem to sell without ads.
Design a holdout: pause or reduce spend for a defined period on a comparable segment.
Compare sales in the holdout period against a matched control period or audience.
Pause or cut permanently only if the holdout shows the spend was not incremental.

test.method: Run the holdout for a pre-registered period and compare sales against the control.

title: Restate the prior month's returns when the return window runs longer than a month
hypothesis: If the prior month gets restated for returns once the full return window closes, on top of the daily accrual, then a category with a long return window (like fashion) does not carry a permanently stale return-rate assumption.
does_not_apply_when: The category's return window closes within the same month as the sale

signal.check: A category has a return window longer than 1 month, but returns are only ever accrued daily with no later restatement once the window closes.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects the accrual once the true return figure is known several weeks later

prerequisites: Return window length by category
steps: Determine the return window for each category (how long customers have to return an item).
Continue the daily accrual at the historical rate for management reads.
Once the full return window for a given month has closed, restate that month's returns to the true figure in the close pack.
Update the accrual rate assumption if the restated figure differs materially.

test.method: Compare the accrued figure against the restated figure for a category with a return window over 30 days.
test.read_point: Once the return window for that month closes

title: Name 1 accountable owner for the revenue forecast, built from the same cohort and spend curves
hypothesis: If 1 person is named accountable for the revenue forecast, built from the cohort curve, the spend curve and the dated calendar, then marketing and finance stop each producing their own separate, disagreeing forecast.

signal.check: Marketing and finance each maintain their own separate revenue forecast, with no single accountable owner reconciling them.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: The cohort curve, spend curve and dated calendar forecast method already in place
steps: Name 1 person (finance or marketing) as the accountable owner of the single revenue forecast.
Require that forecast to be built from the cohort curve, the spend curve and the dated marketing calendar, not a finance extrapolation or a marketing wish.
Route any disagreement about the forecast to that owner for resolution using the shared method.
Retire any separate, parallel forecast maintained by another team.

test.method: Confirm only 1 forecast is being used for planning decisions after the owner is named.

title: State free cash flow's sign convention every time it is reported
hypothesis: If free cash flow is always defined as operating cash flow minus capex stated as a positive number, and that convention is written next to every FCF figure, then nobody accidentally adds back investing cash flow instead of subtracting it.

signal.check: FCF is reported with no stated formula or sign convention, or a model computes it as operating cash flow minus investing cash flow without checking the sign of investing cash flow.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects a sign error that could otherwise inflate reported FCF

prerequisites: Operating cash flow and capex figures
steps: Define FCF as operating cash flow minus capex, with capex stated as a positive number being subtracted.
Check any existing model for the error of adding back a negative investing cash flow instead of subtracting capex directly.
State the formula next to every FCF figure reported.
Fix any model found using the wrong sign convention.

test.method: Recompute FCF for the last 3 months under the correct convention and compare to the prior reported figures.
test.read_point: Once at correction, then every FCF report

title: Model depreciation and tax with the actual payment calendar and loss carryforward, not a flat monthly guess
hypothesis: If depreciation is spread over the correct useful life and tax is modeled against the real payment calendar and accumulated losses, then the cash forecast does not miss a tax lump or misstate how much cash a capitalized cost is really using.

signal.check: The cash forecast treats depreciation as a cash outflow, or spreads tax evenly by month with no reference to the actual payment calendar or loss carryforward.

expected_effect.size: software is commonly depreciated over about 36 months, other assets over 3 or 5 years, per the source

risk.note: Verify useful-life and tax rules with the accountant and a current web check; rules vary by country and policy.

prerequisites: Capitalized cost schedule
Cumulative profit history
Tax payment calendar for the brand's country
steps: Confirm the capitalization policy and useful life for any capitalized software or asset with the accountant.
Spread depreciation over that useful life, but do not treat it as a cash outflow in the cash forecast.
Track cumulative taxable profit against accumulated losses to know when tax becomes payable.
Schedule tax cash outflows on the brand's actual payment calendar, not a flat monthly spread.
Verify the tax calendar and loss carryforward rules for the brand's country with a web check.

test.method: Compare the cash forecast's tax and depreciation lines against actual payments for 1 quarter.

title: Build true CM2 per basket, per SKU and per channel as its own standing report
hypothesis: If CM2 is computed and published per basket, per SKU and per channel as its own standing report, then the CAC ceiling and every pricing or media decision draws from the same, current, correctly scoped margin instead of a stale or blended guess.

signal.check: CM2 is computed ad hoc for a single decision instead of maintained as a standing report broken out by SKU and channel.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Landed cost per SKU (P4)
Fulfillment cost per order
Fee rates
Refund and discount rates by category
steps: Start from price paid by the customer, excluding sales tax.
Subtract landed cost per unit times units in the basket.
Subtract outbound shipping, pick and pack, packing materials, storage and warehouse staff per order.
Subtract payment fees and, for marketplace orders, marketplace fees.
Subtract a refund and discount allowance per order.
Compute CM2 in dollars and percent, repeated per SKU, per channel, and for new-customer baskets only.
Compare the result to whatever margin the team currently quotes, and reset CAC targets off CM2 if the team's number was CM1.

test.method: Compare the standing CM2 report against the ad hoc figure previously used for CAC and pricing decisions.
test.read_point: Every monthly close, and whenever a new SKU or channel launches

title: Build a SKU contribution table ranked by contribution per sale, with inventory and grade columns
hypothesis: If a SKU-level table shows CM2, CAC estimate, contribution per sale, days of inventory and grade side by side, ranked by contribution per sale, then spend and inventory decisions use the same table instead of separate, disconnected views.

signal.check: No single SKU-level table exists showing margin, CAC estimate, contribution per sale and inventory position together.

expected_effect.size: source example: SKU A earned 92 dollars CM at 40 percent while SKU B earned 74 dollars at 61 percent, a gap only visible with SKUs side by side

prerequisites: P5 CM2 build
CAC estimate by product's campaign
Days of inventory by SKU
steps: Compute AOV, product COGS per order, fulfillment per order and CM2 per order overall, per SKU and per category, with a trailing-3-month version.
Divide each fulfillment line by revenue to see which charge moved for each SKU.
Add CAC estimate (campaign CPA, labeled as an estimate) and compute contribution per sale as CM2 minus CAC.
Rank the table by contribution per sale, not by CPA, and flag products whose low CPA hides low contribution.
Add units on hand and days of inventory so the table also supports the inventory grading process.

test.method: Check that the sum of SKU-level revenue in the table ties to net revenue, and that per-order CM2 ties to the P&L ladder.

title: Never code a promo code or automatic discount as ad spend or COGS
hypothesis: If a coupon or automatic discount always reduces revenue instead of landing in ad spend or COGS, then CAC and product margin both stay accurate even when marketing owns the discount and CAC pool.

signal.check: A discount code's value is booked as marketing spend or as a cost of goods line instead of a reduction to revenue.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects an inflated CAC or understated COGS caused by miscoding

prerequisites: Discount codes tracked with a value per redemption
steps: Find every discount code and automatic price reduction currently used.
Confirm each one reduces revenue in the accounting system, not marketing spend or COGS.
Reclassify any miscoded discount.
Check supplier discounts and credits separately; those reduce product cost, not revenue.

test.method: Recompute CAC and product margin after reclassification and compare to the prior figures.

title: Never book ad spend, influencer fees or affiliate commissions as COGS
hypothesis: If ad spend, influencer fees and affiliate commissions always sit in marketing, never in COGS, then product margin is not diluted by costs that only market the product.

signal.check: A partner fee for a partner who only markets the product (not one who ships or picks it) is coded into COGS.

expected_effect.size: unknown, removes a marketing cost wrongly counted as product cost

prerequisites: List of partner and affiliate agreements with what each partner does
steps: List every partner fee: influencers, affiliates, agencies, marketplace revenue-share partners.
For each, decide if the partner ships or picks the product (COGS eligible) or only markets it (never COGS).
Move any marketing-only partner fee out of COGS into variable marketing.
Recompute product margin after the move.

test.method: Recompute CM1 before and after reclassification.

title: Split returns costs by type: return shipping, repackaging and unsellable write-off
hypothesis: If we split return shipping (overhead), repackaging (can be COGS) and unsellable write-off (not COGS) instead of 1 lump return cost, then the margin picture in a high-return category becomes accurate.
does_not_apply_when: Return rate is a small fraction of orders

signal.check: Return rate is above a few percent and all return costs sit in 1 undifferentiated bucket.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Return processing cost data by category
steps: List the return costs the store incurs: shipping back, repackaging, disposal.
Classify return shipping as an overhead expense.
Classify repackaging cost that makes the item sellable again as COGS eligible.
Classify unsellable write-off separately, not as COGS.
Build a returns-cost KPI next to gross margin for high-return categories.

test.method: Track the returns-cost KPI against gross margin for the highest-return category for 1 quarter.

title: Post inbound inventory to stock, move it to COGS only when it sells
hypothesis: If every purchase invoice posts to inventory as an asset and moves to COGS only when the unit sells, then a big purchase order month stops showing a false loss.

signal.check: Purchase invoices are posted straight to expense with no matching stock adjustment.

expected_effect.size: unknown, removes a false loss in months with a large purchase order

risk.note: Bookkeeping correction; may need accounting system setup.

prerequisites: Inventory tracking in the accounting or inventory system
steps: Confirm the accounting system has an inventory asset account, not just an expense account for purchases.
Post every purchase invoice to inventory by SKU and receive date.
Move cost to COGS only when the matching unit sells.
Above a few dozen SKUs or several shipments a month, move from a spreadsheet to inventory software and check totals tie back to invoices.

test.method: Compare reported profit in a large purchase order month before and after the fix.
test.read_point: The next large purchase order month

title: Classify customer support and CX cost as cost of delivery when it scales with orders
hypothesis: If support and CX cost that scales with order volume sits in cost of delivery instead of OPEX, then CM2 is not silently overstated by a cost that grows with sales.
does_not_apply_when: Support cost is a small fixed team with no per-order scaling

signal.check: Support or CX cost is booked entirely to OPEX even though it scales with order or ticket volume.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects CM2 by moving a variable support cost out of OPEX

prerequisites: Support or CX cost broken out by fixed team vs per-order or per-ticket cost
steps: Determine whether support cost scales with order volume (per-order or per-ticket) or is a fixed team cost.
Add the scaling portion to the fulfillment cost formula as cost of delivery.
Keep the fixed team cost in OPEX.
Add the classification to the cost mapping document so it is not silently dropped from CM2.

test.method: Recompute CM2 with support cost included and compare to the prior figure.

title: Classify every cost with the same statutory-vs-internal decision tree
hypothesis: If every account in the chart of accounts is run through the same 9-question classification tree, then statutory COGS and internal cost of delivery stay consistent instead of decided case by case.

signal.check: No written mapping exists from the chart of accounts to statutory COGS, internal cost of delivery, variable marketing or OPEX.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Chart of accounts
Written accounting policy
The accountant's treatment of outbound shipping, packaging and returns
steps: For each account, ask: is it part of buying the product or getting it onto the shelf ready to sell? If yes, statutory COGS.
If unsure, ask: would you have paid this cost if you had not bought these goods? Yes means expense, no means COGS.
Check whether the cost is incurred after the sale, varies with revenue, reduces the price paid, or is marketing.
Route interest below EBITDA and returns costs per their split rule.
Write the final mapping in the brand record and do not change it mid-year.

test.method: Run the checklist in section 5.3 after the mapping is built.

title: Build 1 P&L ladder from gross revenue to net profit with a percent-of-revenue column
hypothesis: If the whole company reads 1 ladder (gross revenue down to net profit, dollars and percent of revenue) every month, then a missed target can be traced instead of argued about.

signal.check: The store has no single ladder view; margins and costs live in scattered spreadsheets or reports.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Gross-to-net data by day
Landed cost table
Fulfillment cost per order
OPEX by account
A written variable vs fixed marketing convention
steps: List every ladder line: gross revenue, discounts, refunds, chargebacks, shipping collected, net revenue, product COGS, CM1, fulfillment, CM2, variable marketing, CM3, OPEX, EBITDA, interest, tax, D&A, net profit.
Compute each line for the month in dollars and as a percent of net revenue.
Add a per-order column and a trailing-3-month per-order column.
Set a target per line from the owner's net profit target and OPEX plan.
Check the 4 buckets sum to 100 percent and CM2 percent ties to the unit-economics view.

test.method: Build the ladder for 1 month and check it against the 4 standing checks (bucket sum, CM2 tie-out, net revenue reconciliation, margin labels).

title: Build the 4-bucket P&L and name the 1 bucket most out of line
hypothesis: If every month we split revenue into cost of delivery, CAC, OPEX and profit and compare to a reference mix, then the store works on the 1 bucket eating profit instead of cutting everything at once.

signal.check: No monthly view breaks revenue into these 4 buckets, or the buckets are treated as targets rather than flags.

expected_effect.size: reference mix in the source: cost of delivery 30 to 40 percent, CAC 25 to 30 percent, OPEX 10 to 15 percent, profit 15 to 20 percent

prerequisites: P1 P&L ladder built
steps: Compute cost of delivery, CAC (pure variable media), OPEX and profit as shares of net revenue.
Compare the shares to the reference mix, remembering industry average COGS is about 58 percent.
Name the 1 bucket most out of line for this store's own history and category.
Apply the fault rule only to that bucket's lines, not to the whole P&L.

test.method: Track the 4 bucket shares for 3 months and confirm the flagged bucket improves after action.

title: Trace every missed target to the line above it before reacting (the fault rule)
hypothesis: If a missed EBITDA, CM3 or CM2 target is always traced to the specific line above it before any budget is cut, then the fix targets the real cause instead of an easy but wrong lever.

signal.check: A budget or headcount cut follows a missed target with no written trace of which line above it caused the miss.

expected_effect.size: source example: a loss month was traced to marketing rising from 29 to 39 percent of revenue

prerequisites: P&L ladder with monthly history
steps: For a missed EBITDA, check OPEX, marketing and cost of delivery first.
For a missed CM3, check marketing and cost of delivery.
For a missed CM2, check cost of delivery and revenue (refunds, discounts, shipping collected).
Write the constraint, the lever and the owner before proposing any cut.

test.method: Review 3 months of miss investigations and confirm each names a specific line above the miss.

title: Write a fixed rule for what counts as variable vs fixed marketing, and keep it all year
hypothesis: If we write down which marketing costs are variable (above CM3) and which are fixed (in OPEX) and never move them mid-year, then CM3 and the CAC bucket stay comparable month to month.

signal.check: Creative, agency or retainer costs move between variable marketing and OPEX from month to month with no written rule.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: List of all marketing-related cost accounts
steps: List every marketing cost: paid ads, influencers, events, agency and creative help.
Decide which ones flex with demand (variable, above CM3) and which are permanent team or retainer cost (fixed, OPEX).
Write the rule down and share it with finance and marketing.
Do not move a cost between buckets mid-year; if the convention changes, note it and hold it for a full year.

test.method: Check that the same accounts sit in the same bucket for 12 consecutive months.

title: Reinvest profit through marketing before headcount, software or office spend
hypothesis: If OPEX growth is held back and marketing is the first reinvestment lever, then profit stops going flat in dollars for years while OPEX quietly outpaces revenue.

signal.check: OPEX percent of revenue is flat or rising while revenue grows, or new headcount, software and office spend keep adding up before marketing gets more budget.

expected_effect.size: source claims OPEX outpaces marketing and cost of delivery growth at most 7-figure brands, with profit flat in dollars for 3 to 4 years

risk.note: A hiring or spending freeze is reversible, unlike a bad hire.

prerequisites: OPEX and revenue trend for the last 12 months
steps: Chart OPEX percent of revenue against revenue growth for the last 12 months.
If OPEX percent is flat or rising while revenue grows, freeze non-revenue hires, software and office spend.
Redirect the next dollar of reinvestment into marketing instead of headcount.
Re-check the trend after 1 quarter.

test.method: Compare OPEX percent of revenue before and after the freeze for 1 quarter.

title: Add a percent-of-revenue column to every ladder and bucket line every month
hypothesis: If every ladder and bucket line carries a percent-of-revenue column, then a rising marketing percent while scaling reads differently from a rising cost-of-delivery or OPEX percent, which should hold steady.

signal.check: The monthly ladder or bucket view shows only dollars, with no percent-of-revenue column.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: P1 P&L ladder built
steps: Add a percent-of-net-revenue column next to every dollar line in the ladder and bucket view.
Read a rising marketing percent as expected during scaling.
Read a rising cost-of-delivery or OPEX percent as a flag, since those should hold steady.
Review the percent columns every month before the dollar columns.

test.method: Track which lines move as a percent of revenue over 3 months and confirm the marketing-vs-fixed-cost distinction holds.

title: Track net shipping cost and flag it once it passes 20 percent of revenue
hypothesis: If we track net shipping cost (shipping collected minus outbound shipping cost) every month, then a shipping line drifting toward 20 to 30 percent of revenue gets caught and tested instead of ignored.

signal.check: Net shipping cost is not tracked monthly, or shipping cost sits above 10 percent of revenue with no flag raised.

expected_effect.size: shipping should run about 10 percent of revenue or less; 20 to 30 percent is a red flag in the source

risk.note: Monitoring step; any shipping charge change is tested separately in conversion rate optimization.

prerequisites: Shipping collected and outbound shipping cost by month
steps: Compute net shipping cost = shipping collected minus outbound shipping cost, monthly.
Divide by net revenue to get shipping percent.
Flag any month where shipping percent exceeds 20 percent for review.
Hand a shipping-charge change to the conversion rate optimization track as a test, not a blanket change.

test.method: Track shipping percent for 3 months and compare against the 10 to 30 percent bands.

title: Report revenue, profit and cash as 3 separate numbers, never as 1 story
hypothesis: If revenue, profit and cash are reported as 3 separate lines every month, then a growth plan stops assuming margin will expand later while cash quietly runs out.

signal.check: A growth plan or investor update only talks about revenue growth, with no separate line for profit percent and cash position.

expected_effect.size: source example: a 10 million dollar business at 5 percent net makes 500,000; a 5 million dollar business at 20 percent net makes 1,000,000

prerequisites: Monthly P&L and cash balance
steps: Add net profit percent and closing cash balance next to revenue on every report.
Reject any growth plan that shows revenue targets with no profit or cash line.
Ask, for any revenue growth plan, what happens to profit percent and cash if margin does not expand.
Review all 3 numbers together at every monthly and quarterly review.

test.method: Check that the next 3 monthly reports show revenue, profit percent and cash balance together.

title: Make daily contribution margin the whole team's scoreboard, cash the CEO's own
hypothesis: If daily cm3_media is reported against a monthly goal for the whole team, and a separate rolling 13-week cash forecast stays with the CEO or CFO, then everyone manages the number they can actually move.

signal.check: Daily ad spend exists but no daily contribution margin dashboard exists, or cash forecasting is mixed into the daily team view.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Daily gross revenue, product cost, fulfillment cost and ad spend
steps: Build a daily cm3_media dashboard visible to the whole team.
Set a monthly CM goal sized to cover fixed costs.
Keep a separate rolling 13-week cash flow forecast owned only by the CEO or CFO.
Do not let daily CM pressure drive short-term cuts that ignore the cash forecast.

test.method: Run both views for 1 month and check the team responds to CM while cash decisions stay with the owner.
test.read_point: Daily for CM, weekly for cash

title: Remove fixed costs from the daily contribution view
hypothesis: If rent and payroll are kept out of the daily contribution view, then the team stops seeing a false cut-spend signal on ordinary days when media is actually still profitable.

signal.check: The daily dashboard spreads monthly fixed costs across days, producing negative daily profit even when media makes positive contribution.

expected_effect.size: unknown, removes a false negative signal caused by spread fixed costs

prerequisites: Daily contribution dashboard built
steps: Remove rent, payroll and other fixed costs from the daily dashboard formula.
Keep only revenue, product cost, fulfillment cost and ad spend in the daily view.
Carry OPEX only in the monthly view.
If media makes positive incremental CM on an ordinary day, do not treat it as a loss day.

test.method: Compare the daily CM read with and without fixed costs spread across days.

title: Read the dashboard top down: cash, then CM, then business, then customer, then channel metrics
hypothesis: If every dashboard and alert follows the order cash, contribution margin, business metrics, customer metrics, channel metrics, then a win at one level does not hide a loss at another, such as CM up while the new-customer file shrinks.

signal.check: Reports lead with channel ROAS or revenue instead of cash and contribution margin, or no fixed order exists across dashboards.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Cash forecast, CM dashboard, business, customer and channel metrics all built
steps: Order every dashboard and report: cash flow, then contribution margin, then business metrics (revenue, spend, MER, AOV), then customer metrics (new-customer revenue, aMER), then channel metrics (platform ROAS).
Set alerts to fire on divergence between levels, such as CM rising while the new-customer file shrinks.
Reject any report that leads with channel ROAS.
Apply the same order to every new dashboard built.

test.method: Review the last month for a case where 1 level looked healthy while another did not.

title: Stop using daily or weekly ROAS as the core acquisition decision tool
hypothesis: If aMER, profit contribution and windowed LTGP:CAC replace daily ROAS as the acquisition decision tool, then budget moves stop chasing a within-platform number that does not reflect true profitability.

signal.check: Budget decisions are made off daily or weekly platform ROAS with no aMER or LTGP:CAC view in front of them.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: aMER and LTGP:CAC computed and available live
steps: Build a live view of aMER and profit contribution, and ideally LTGP:CAC in a fixed window.
Use platform ROAS only for directional reads inside 1 platform.
Route any budget decision through the aMER and LTGP:CAC view first.
Retrain the team that ROAS answers a narrower question than aMER.

test.method: Compare a budget decision made off ROAS alone against the same decision using aMER and LTGP:CAC.

title: Split every finance-grade metric into new-customer and blended versions
hypothesis: If MER, CM, cohort size and first-order GP are all reported in a new-customer version alongside the blended version, then acquisition decisions stop using a number contaminated by returning revenue that would have come anyway.

signal.check: Reports show MER or CM only in blended form, with no new-customer-only version alongside it.

expected_effect.size: source example: MER of 2 while aMER might be 1.4

prerequisites: New vs returning flag on every order
steps: Tag every order as new or returning based on first-order date from store data.
Compute new-customer revenue, aMER, new-customer CM and new-customer cohort size alongside their blended versions.
Add first-order gross profit as its own line.
Report both versions side by side in every readout, never blended alone.

test.method: Compare blended MER to aMER for the current month and note the gap.

title: Track the active customer file, not cumulative customers, to set new-customer goals
hypothesis: If we track customers active in the last 6 to 8 months instead of all-time customers, then new-customer goals are set against the real base instead of squeezing an already-tapped list.

signal.check: Customer counts reported are cumulative all-time totals, with no active-file definition or trend.

expected_effect.size: about 80 percent of customers who will ever return do so within 6 to 8 months, per the source's portfolio heuristic

risk.note: Reporting change only; verify against the brand's own repurchase curve first.

prerequisites: Order history with customer id and order date
The brand's own repurchase curve, if available
steps: Define the active file as customers who ordered in the last 6 to 8 months, checked against the brand's own repurchase curve.
Track the size of the active file monthly, separate from cumulative customers.
Set new-customer acquisition goals against the active file's growth, not the cumulative total.
Flag any month where revenue rises while the active file shrinks.

test.method: Track the active file size for 3 months and compare its trend to new-customer acquisition goals.

title: Track actuals against a daily expectation so a miss is seen by day 5, not day 22
hypothesis: If actual revenue is tracked against a daily expected-revenue line, then a monthly miss is caught by day 5 instead of discovered at month end.

signal.check: The store only compares actual revenue to target at month end, with no daily expectation line.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: The 3-model daily expectation (new-customer, returning, event effect)
steps: Build the daily expected revenue line from the 3-model forecast.
Track actual revenue against expected revenue daily.
Flag any day where the variance is material and name the likely cause.
Act on a miss by day 5 of the month instead of waiting for month end.

test.method: Track the day the first material miss was caught for 2 consecutive months.

title: Build a daily contribution dashboard with returns accrued at the historical rate
hypothesis: If the daily contribution dashboard uses accrued returns instead of processed returns, and drops fixed costs, then the daily cm3_media number is not distorted by return timing or spread fixed costs.

signal.check: No daily contribution dashboard exists, or the one that exists uses processed refunds and includes fixed costs.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Daily gross revenue, discounts, shipping collected, orders with new flag, ad spend, product cost, fulfillment cost, historical return rate
steps: Compute daily net revenue with refunds accrued at the historical rate, not processed refunds.
Compute daily cm3_media = net revenue minus product COGS minus fulfillment minus ad spend.
Set a monthly CM goal and a daily pacing line from OPEX plus the profit target.
Order rows below CM as revenue, spend, MER, AOV, then new-customer metrics, then channel ROAS last.
At month end, true up accrued refunds to processed refunds and post the difference.

test.method: Check that month-to-date cm3_media ties to the monthly ladder within the accrual difference.

title: Publish a weekly profit memo covering CM, new vs returning, variance and inventory risk
hypothesis: If a 1-page weekly memo covers CM, new vs returning split, variance cause, inventory risk and cash, then the owner catches a problem inside the week instead of at month end.

signal.check: No weekly memo exists that pulls CM, new vs returning revenue, variance and inventory risk into 1 place.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Daily contribution dashboard
Cohort forecast
Inventory days-of-stock by SKU
Cash forecast
steps: Report week and month-to-date net revenue, CM2, cm3_media and cm3_loaded against goal.
Split new vs returning: new-customer revenue, aMER, first-order GP, CM:CAC, count vs goal; returning revenue vs cohort forecast.
Name the variance cause using the fault rule.
Report top-10 SKU days of stock vs lead time and any sell-out risk.
Report cash balance, lowest projected point in 13 weeks, and any alerts fired with a recommended action.

test.method: Run the memo for 4 consecutive weeks and check every number carries its definition and period.

title: Accrue returns at the historical rate daily, then true up at month end
hypothesis: If daily and monthly revenue subtract an accrued return rate instead of waiting for processed refunds, then the efficiency read stays accurate instead of spiking when old returns land in a later month.
does_not_apply_when: Return rate is a negligible share of gross revenue

signal.check: Revenue efficiency reads use processed refunds instead of an accrued return rate, or no return-rate history has been set.

expected_effect.size: source example: a 1,000,000 dollar December accrues 100,000 in returns, about 3,333 a day

prerequisites: Return rate by month, and by category where it differs
steps: Set the return rate from history, by category if rates differ meaningfully.
Subtract accrued returns (rate times the day's revenue) from daily and monthly revenue.
At month end, true up accrued returns to actual processed returns and post the difference.
Restate the prior month in the close pack if the return window runs longer than a month.

test.method: Compare the accrued-return revenue read against the processed-return read for a post-peak month.
test.read_point: Monthly, with special attention right after a peak season

title: Never read platform default total sales as the efficiency base right after a peak season
hypothesis: If the efficiency base always uses accrued returns instead of the platform's default total-sales figure, then a spike in processed peak-season returns stops triggering a wrong spend pullback the next month.

signal.check: A post-peak month (like January) shows a spike in the apparent return rate using the platform's default sales metric.

expected_effect.size: source example: a 500,000 dollar January that processes 100,000 of December returns looks like a 20 percent return rate when the true rate is 10 percent

risk.note: Reporting correction only; verify the platform's exact default metric.

prerequisites: Accrued returns method already in place
steps: Confirm what the store platform's default sales metric includes.
Replace it with order revenue using the accrued return rate for any efficiency read.
Flag any January or post-peak month specifically for this check.
Do not pull back ad spend based on the platform's default figure alone.

test.method: Recompute the return rate for the last post-peak month using accrued vs platform-default methods and compare.

title: Put a refund and discount allowance into every per-basket margin and price calculation
hypothesis: If a refund and discount allowance is subtracted from every per-basket margin and the pricing waterfall, then CM2 and the CAC ceiling are not overstated by ignoring expected returns.

signal.check: CM2 or the pricing waterfall does not subtract a refund and discount allowance by category.

expected_effect.size: source example: about 5 percent discounts plus about 10 percent refunds in a t-shirt example; fashion refund rates run 10 to 80 percent

prerequisites: Refund rate and average discount rate by category
steps: Compute refund rate and average discount rate by category.
Subtract both as a combined allowance from every per-basket CM2 calculation.
Include the same allowance in the pricing waterfall for new products.
Update the allowance whenever the category's refund pattern changes materially.

test.method: Recompute CM2 with and without the allowance and compare the gap by category.
test.read_point: Every CM2 build and price review

title: Track chargebacks and disputes as their own line, separate from processed refunds
hypothesis: If chargebacks and payment disputes get their own count and rate, separate from refunds, then a rising dispute rate is caught early as a fraud or payment-processor risk signal.

signal.check: Chargebacks are lumped into the general refunds line with no separate count or rate tracked.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Payment processor chargeback data by month
steps: Pull chargebacks and disputes as their own line from the payment processor.
Compute a chargeback rate separate from the processed refund rate.
Track the rate monthly and flag any sustained rise.
Escalate a rising rate as a possible fraud or processor risk signal, not just a revenue adjustment.

test.method: Track the chargeback rate for 3 months and compare against the store's baseline.

title: Compute CAC only from customers whose first order fell in the period, from the store's own data
hypothesis: If CAC always divides by new customers counted from the store's own order data, never platform CPA or all orders, then the acquisition efficiency number stops flattering itself.

signal.check: CAC is reported using platform-attributed new customers or total orders instead of the store's own new-customer count.
