expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects an understated CAC caused by platform CPA or all-order denominators

prerequisites: New vs returning flag on every order from the store platform
steps: Count customers whose first order fell in the period, from the store's own order data.
Divide total variable marketing spend by that count to get CAC.
Remove any CAC figure computed from platform-reported CPA or total order count.
Label the CAC figure with its exact denominator.

test.method: Compare the store-data CAC against the platform CPA for the same period.

title: Report 4 labeled CACs: blended, media-only, paid, fully loaded
hypothesis: If every CAC report shows blended, media-only, paid and fully loaded CAC with labels, then the daily media decision and the payback or pricing decision each use the right number instead of 1 ambiguous figure.

signal.check: Only 1 unlabeled CAC number is used for both daily media steering and payback or pricing decisions.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Ad spend, other variable marketing, and first-order discount cost tracked separately
steps: Compute cac_media = ad spend divided by new customers.
Compute cac_blended = all variable marketing divided by new customers.
Compute cac_paid = paid spend divided by paid-attributed new customers.
Compute cac_loaded = ad spend plus influencers, affiliates, variable agency and creative, plus first-order discount cost, divided by new customers.
Label every CAC figure in every report with which of the 4 it is.

test.method: Check that every CAC figure appearing in a report or dashboard for 1 month carries its label.

title: Treat channel-level CAC as a planning estimate only, never a finance number
hypothesis: If channel-level CAC is used only for planning estimates and never appears in the P&L, then a per-channel attribution guess does not get treated as a real cost number.

signal.check: A per-channel CAC line appears in the P&L or is treated as decision-grade without an incrementality calibration.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: cpc and conversion rate by channel for the planning estimate
steps: Compute cac_from_funnel = cpc divided by conversion rate as a rough planning estimate only.
Never place a channel-level CAC line inside the P&L.
Calibrate any channel comparison with an incrementality factor where a test exists.
Use channel CAC for planning and channel comparison discussions only.

test.method: Search the current P&L for any per-channel CAC line and remove it if present.

title: Pair every CAC target with new-customer first-order gross profit, not blended AOV
hypothesis: If CAC is always paired with new-customer AOV and first-order gross profit instead of blended AOV times blended margin, then a CAC target stops looking fine on paper while losing money on every new customer.

signal.check: A CAC target was set using blended AOV and blended margin instead of new-customer AOV and first-order GP.

expected_effect.size: source example: blended 100 dollars times 70 percent gives a 70 dollar GP and a 35 dollar CAC target, but new-customer AOV was 90 dollars with about 50 dollars first-order GP

risk.note: A corrected, tighter CAC target may require lowering live bids.

prerequisites: New-customer AOV and first-order gross profit computed separately from blended figures
steps: Compute new-customer AOV and first-order gross profit for new customers only.
Set the CAC target from these figures, not from blended AOV times blended margin.
Recheck any live CAC target that was set off blended figures.
Document the new-customer basis next to the CAC target.

test.method: Recompute the CAC target using new-customer figures and compare it to the current live target.

title: Report paid CAC separately from blended CAC when organic includes friends and family
hypothesis: If paid CAC is reported next to blended CAC, then a scaling decision does not rely on an organic channel that cannot scale, hiding a much thinner paid efficiency.
does_not_apply_when: Organic acquisition is a meaningfully scalable channel, not friends and family or brand loyalty alone

signal.check: Only blended CAC or blended LTV:CAC is reported, with no paid-only version, ahead of a scale-up decision.

expected_effect.size: source example: blended LTV:CAC was 1.4 while paid LTV:CAC was 1.08

prerequisites: Paid spend and paid-attributed new customers tracked separately from organic
steps: Compute cac_paid = paid spend divided by paid-attributed new customers.
Compute LTV:CAC using cac_paid alongside the blended version.
Before any scaling decision, check the paid-only number, not just blended.
Flag any large gap between blended and paid CAC to the owner before raising budget.

test.method: Compare blended and paid CAC and LTV:CAC for the current quarter.

title: Set the CAC or ROAS line from unit economics and payback, then hold it
hypothesis: If the CAC or ROAS line is set once from unit economics and payback, and held rather than lowered whenever the team cannot hit it, then acquisition spend does not slide into unprofitable territory a step at a time.

signal.check: The CAC or ROAS line has been lowered more than once in the last few quarters with no change in underlying unit economics.

expected_effect.size: a 2021 partner analysis the source cites found 60 percent of media dollars never paid back over any period

risk.note: Holding the line may mean lower near-term volume; requires owner buy-in.

prerequisites: Break-even CAC and payback window computed from real unit economics
steps: Set the CAC or ROAS line from break-even economics (F15) and the payback window, not from a wish.
Require an explicit owner decision to change the line, logged with a reason.
When the line cannot be hit, solve with story, creative, offer, product or new channels instead of lowering it.
Review the line's history quarterly to confirm it has not drifted down without a decision.

test.method: Review the CAC or ROAS line's change history for the last 4 quarters and confirm each change has an owner decision attached.

title: Stop scaling spend when CAC rises but CM and repeat orders stay flat
hypothesis: If spend growth is paused whenever CAC keeps rising with flat CM and flat repeat orders, then the store avoids funding a widening loss on every new customer.

signal.check: CAC has risen for 2 or more consecutive periods while CM per order and lifetime orders per customer stayed flat.

expected_effect.size: source example: CAC rose 68 to 79 to 123 to 149 with flat CM and 1.2 to 1.8 lifetime orders, CM:CAC around 0.58 to 0.6

risk.note: Pausing spend growth trades near-term volume for unit economics; needs owner sign-off.

prerequisites: CAC, CM per order and lifetime orders tracked over at least 3 periods
steps: Track CAC, CM per order and lifetime orders per customer over the last 3 to 4 periods.
If CAC is rising while CM and lifetime orders stay flat, pause spend growth.
Fix the underlying first-order economics or repeat rate before scaling again.
Do not fund the gap with new fundraising as a substitute for fixing unit economics.

test.method: Track CM:CAC over the following quarter after the pause and confirm it stabilizes or improves.

title: Screen new-customer counts for fraud and bot orders before they feed CAC
hypothesis: If new-customer counts are screened for fraud, bot orders and duplicate accounts first, then CAC and the cohort table are not distorted by orders that were never real customers.
does_not_apply_when: The store has low paid-acquisition volume and no fraud signal

signal.check: No fraud or bot screening step exists between order data and the new-customer count used for CAC.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects an understated CAC caused by counting non-real new customers

risk.note: Screening step; verify against brand fraud tooling before use.

prerequisites: Order and account data with fraud or bot signals available
steps: Identify a fraud or bot-detection signal available from the payment processor or fraud tool.
Filter new-customer counts to exclude flagged orders before computing CAC.
Filter the same records out of the cohort table.
Review the filtered volume monthly to see if fraud share is rising.

test.method: Compare CAC computed with and without the fraud filter for 1 month.

title: Gate acquisition on first-order CM2:CAC at or above 1, unless a proven cohort tail justifies more
hypothesis: If the store requires CM2 per new order divided by CAC to be 1 or above by default, then a buy-once category or an unproven repeat business does not fund acquisition that never gets paid back.
does_not_apply_when: A cohort of 6 or more months proves cumulative gross profit exceeds CAC and cash can carry the payback

signal.check: The store spends on acquisition with first-order CM2:CAC below 1 and no cohort data proving a repeat tail.

expected_effect.size: source flags first-order GP under about 70 dollars as probably a problem for paid acquisition at scale

risk.note: Cutting spend to fit the gate can reduce near-term volume.

prerequisites: First-order CM2 and CAC computed for new customers
steps: Compute first-order CM2 per new order and divide by CAC.
If the ratio is below 1 and no proven cohort tail exists, treat it as a default fail.
Fix first-order economics (price, offer, cost of delivery) before spending further.
Only exceed the gate with a cohort of at least 6 months showing cumulative gross profit above CAC.

test.method: Track first-order CM2:CAC monthly and flag any month it falls below 1 without a documented cohort exception.

title: Report LTV as lifetime gross profit, never as lifetime revenue
hypothesis: If LTV is always computed as CM2 per order times lifetime orders instead of revenue, then a spending decision built on LTV does not overstate how much a customer is really worth.

signal.check: LTV is quoted or pulled from a tool as a revenue figure rather than a gross-profit figure.

expected_effect.size: unknown, revenue-based LTV and profit-based LTV can differ by a wide margin

prerequisites: Cohort table with CM2 per order by month since first purchase
steps: Confirm whether any LTV figure currently in use is revenue-based or profit-based.
Rebuild LTV as cumulative CM2 per customer from the cohort table.
Replace any revenue-based LTV figure in dashboards or tools with the corrected figure.
Label every LTV figure as gross profit, not revenue.

test.method: Compare the revenue-based LTV figure against the corrected gross-profit LTV for the same cohort.
test.read_point: Once at correction, then part of every LTV report

title: Time-box every LTV and LTGP figure to a stated window
hypothesis: If every LTV or LTGP figure states its window (30, 90, 180 or 365 days, or the cohort's plateau month), then acquisition spend is not justified by an open-ended number that keeps rising the longer you wait.

signal.check: An LTV or LTGP figure is used to justify spend with no stated time window.

expected_effect.size: source example: 100 dollars at 6 months, 110 at 12, 120 at 18, growing the longer the window runs

prerequisites: Cohort table with cumulative gross profit by month since first purchase
steps: Compute LTGP at 30 and 90 days for efficiency targets.
Compute LTV at 90 or 180 days for customer value, and 365 days only when acquisition is aggressive.
Find the plateau month where cumulative cohort revenue stops rising and use it as the ceiling window for long-cycle products.
Reject any LTV or LTGP number in a report with no stated window.

test.method: Audit the last 5 reports that cited an LTV figure and confirm each states its window.

title: Build retention and LTV only from cohorts, never from aggregate totals
hypothesis: If retention, LTV and payback are always read from a cohort table grouped by first-purchase month, then the shape of the retention curve is visible instead of hidden inside an aggregate churn rate.

signal.check: Retention or LTV claims are based on an aggregate churn rate or a calendar-month total instead of a cohort table.

expected_effect.size: source example: Dollar Shave Club lost about 25 percent in month 1 and about 10 points across all of year 2, a pattern an aggregate rate hides

prerequisites: Order history with customer id and order date
steps: Group customers by first-purchase month into cohorts.
Build retention, revenue and orders grids by cohort and month since first order, dividing by the original cohort size.
Leave future cells empty rather than filling with 0.
Read a calendar month diagonally across cohorts, and compare cohorts at the same age to spot a weak one.

test.method: Check that a calendar month's total ties to the diagonal sum across cohorts.

title: Only spend above first-order profit when a 6-month-plus cohort proves the tail
hypothesis: If spend above first-order CM2 is allowed only when a cohort of at least 6 months shows cumulative gross profit passing CAC, then the store does not assume a retention story it has not actually observed.
does_not_apply_when: No cohort has 6 or more months of history yet

signal.check: CAC is being spent above first-order CM2 with no cohort of at least 6 months confirming the payback.

expected_effect.size: source example: 115 dollar CAC against 33 dollar first-order GP accepted because cumulative GP passed CAC at purchase 4

risk.note: Spending above first-order profit without real proof can burn cash quickly; requires cash to carry the payback.

prerequisites: Cohort table with at least 6 months of history
Cash forecast confirming the payback can be carried
steps: Pull the cohort with the most history, at least 6 months.
Compute cumulative gross profit per customer against the CAC outlay.
Confirm the cash forecast can carry the payback period before approving overspend.
Use the lifetime-orders figure from the proven cohort, never an extrapolation.

test.method: Track the cohort's cumulative gross profit against CAC monthly until payback is confirmed or fails.
test.read_point: Monthly, over the cohort's payback window

title: Read LTGP:CAC in a fixed window against the bands, and test marginal spend above 3
hypothesis: If LTGP:CAC is read in a fixed 30 or 90 day window and a ratio above 3 triggers a marginal spend test instead of an assumption of underspending, then the store neither underspends nor overspends against its real retention.

signal.check: LTGP:CAC is reported with no fixed window, or a ratio above 3 has not prompted a marginal-spend test.

expected_effect.size: 2 to 3 is read as optimal; below 1 is losing money on acquisition; above 3 prompts a marginal test before more spend

risk.note: Diagnostic step; the resulting spend change is a separate decision.

prerequisites: Cohort cumulative gross profit at 30 and 90 days
cac_media and cac_loaded
steps: Compute cumulative gross profit per customer at 30 and 90 days from the cohort table.
Divide by cac_media and report against the bands (below 1 losing, 1 to 2 weak, 2 to 3 optimal, above 3 a flag).
If above 3, run the marginal spend test before recommending more budget.
If below 1, check first-order gross profit and cost of delivery before calling it a lifetime play.

test.method: Run the marginal spend test (incremental spend vs incremental new-customer revenue) whenever LTGP:CAC exceeds 3.
test.read_point: Whenever the ratio crosses a band

title: Treat LTGP:CAC below 1 as a first-order economics problem, not a lifetime-value strategy
hypothesis: If any LTGP:CAC reading below 1 in the 90-day window triggers a review of price, offer and cost of delivery instead of a wait-for-lifetime-value story, then a real acquisition loss gets fixed instead of excused.

signal.check: LTGP:CAC in the 90-day window is below 1 and has been explained away as a lifetime-value play with no cohort proof.

expected_effect.size: unknown

risk.note: Diagnostic and pricing review, not a live spend change by itself.

prerequisites: LTGP:CAC computed in the 90-day window
steps: Confirm the 90-day LTGP:CAC reading is below 1.
Review price, offer structure and cost of delivery for the affected product or channel.
Only accept the below-1 reading as a lifetime play if a proven 6-month-plus cohort shows a repayment tail.
Fix the first-order economics before increasing spend further.

test.method: Track the 90-day LTGP:CAC after the fix for 1 to 2 more cohorts.

title: Compute CAC payback from a real cohort, never CAC divided by monthly gross profit
hypothesis: If CAC payback is computed from actual cohort survivorship instead of the naive CAC-over-monthly-GP shortcut, then the payback window used for decisions is not understated by ignoring churn.

signal.check: Payback is quoted as CAC divided by monthly gross profit, with no cohort survivorship applied.

expected_effect.size: source example: naive payback 3.2 months vs cohort payback 8 months

prerequisites: Cohort table with survivors and gross profit per period
steps: Pick 1 cohort of known size and compute the outlay (cohort size times CAC).
Sum cumulative gross profit period by period using actual survivors, not an assumed 0 churn.
Find the first period where cumulative gross profit meets or exceeds the outlay.
Report the naive figure only as a stated lower bound, never as the real payback.

test.method: Compare the naive payback figure against the cohort-based payback figure for the same cohort.
test.read_point: Each new cohort with enough history

title: Read the profit tail after payback, not just whether it breaks even
hypothesis: If we read how much profit accrues after a cohort's CAC payback point, then a cohort that barely breaks even with no tail gets flagged as a pricing or fundamentals problem instead of a false pass.

signal.check: Payback is reported as pass or fail with no tail-profit figure computed after the break-even point.

expected_effect.size: source example: a 125 dollar CAC broke even by month 5, a 225 dollar CAC by month 11 in the same model

prerequisites: Cohort payback already computed
steps: After finding the payback period, keep summing cumulative gross profit to the plateau month.
Subtract the CAC outlay to get tail profit.
Test CAC sensitivity: what CAC still breaks even by month 5 vs month 11.
Flag any cohort with a thin or zero tail for a pricing or fundamentals review.

test.method: Compare tail profit across the last 2 to 3 cohorts to see if it is growing or shrinking.

title: Set the CAC payback window with the owner from the cash reserve, 3 to 6 months as the default limit
hypothesis: If the acceptable payback window is set explicitly with the owner based on cash reserve, defaulting to 3 to 6 months, then acquisition spend does not quietly assume a longer payback than the business can actually carry.

signal.check: No agreed payback window exists, or spend implies a payback longer than 6 months with no cash-reserve check.

expected_effect.size: agencies, CPG, fashion and retail commonly run 3 to 6 months per the source

risk.note: Setting a strict window may mean turning down otherwise-attractive spend; needs owner agreement.

prerequisites: Cash reserve and owner's payback tolerance discussed
steps: Ask the owner directly how many months of payback the cash reserve can carry.
Set the default window at 3 to 6 months unless the owner explicitly extends it.
Check any planned spend increase against the agreed window before approving it.
Revisit the window whenever the cash position changes materially.

test.method: Track whether spend decisions stay inside the agreed payback window for 1 quarter.

title: Report new-customer and returning-customer profit contribution as 2 separate lines
hypothesis: If new-customer and returning-customer profit contribution are reported separately every month, then the team sees which segment is actually carrying the business instead of reading 1 blended profit figure.

signal.check: Monthly profit is reported as 1 blended figure with no split between new and returning customer contribution.

expected_effect.size: source example: 140,000 dollars new revenue at 50 percent GM minus 50,000 ad spend equals 20,000; 60,000 returning at 50 percent minus 2,500 retention tools equals 27,500

prerequisites: New vs returning revenue and cost split already tracked
steps: Split net revenue, cost of delivery and marketing cost between new and returning customers.
Compute profit contribution separately for each segment.
Report both segments side by side every month.
Discuss which segment is driving profit before setting next month's priorities.

test.method: Track the split for 3 months and see which segment's contribution trend changes the story.

title: Judge marketing percent of revenue against the brand's own repeat curve, not a universal number
hypothesis: If marketing spend as a percent of revenue is judged against the brand's own LTV and repeat curve instead of a universal target, then the marketing budget matches the brand's real retention instead of copying an unrelated brand's mix.

signal.check: Marketing percent of revenue is being compared to an external benchmark with no reference to the brand's own repeat rate or LTV.

expected_effect.size: low-LTV hard goods often run 40 to 50 percent; legacy retailers with strong repeat run about 10 percent, per the source

prerequisites: Repeat rate and LTV computed for the brand
steps: Compute the brand's own repeat rate and LTV.
Plot marketing percent of revenue against that repeat curve over the last 12 months.
Judge whether the current marketing percent fits a brand at this repeat-rate stage.
Avoid copying another brand's marketing percent without checking its repeat curve.

test.method: Track marketing percent of revenue against repeat rate for 2 consecutive quarters.

title: Only hold CAC flat for a repeat order when nothing was spent to get it
hypothesis: If retargeting-driven repeat orders carry their own CAC instead of assuming 0 acquisition cost, then LTV:CAC does not overstate value from customers who were paid to come back.

signal.check: LTV:CAC treats every repeat order as free, even when paid retargeting spend drove some of them.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects an overstated LTV:CAC when retargeting spend is currently ignored

prerequisites: Retargeting spend tracked separately from acquisition spend
steps: Check whether repeat orders came through free channels (email, organic) or paid retargeting.
For free-channel repeat orders, keep CAC at 0 for that order in lifetime CM.
For paid-retargeting-driven repeat orders, add that spend into the lifetime CM calculation.
Recompute LTV:CAC with the corrected attribution.

test.method: Recompute LTV:CAC with and without retargeting spend included and compare.

title: Work retention first, then AOV, then COGS renegotiation, as the LTV lever order
hypothesis: If retention is worked before AOV and COGS renegotiation, then LTV grows through the lever the source found had the largest effect, instead of chasing a smaller renegotiation win first.

signal.check: The team is focused on renegotiating COGS or raising AOV while churn has not been addressed.

expected_effect.size: source example: cutting churn from 27 percent to 20 percent raised churn-based LTV 35 percent; renegotiated COGS lifted LTV from 69 to about 80 dollars in the same case

risk.note: Prioritization guidance; the actual retention work is a separate project.

prerequisites: Churn rate, AOV and COGS all tracked for the subscription base
steps: Compute current churn rate, AOV and COGS for the subscription base.
Prioritize a churn-reduction project before an AOV or COGS renegotiation project.
Compete on value delivered, not price, since price-led buyers stay price sensitive.
Recompute LTV after the churn project to confirm the expected lift.

test.method: Compare LTV before and after a churn-reduction project, holding AOV and COGS constant.
test.read_point: 1 to 2 quarters after the churn project

title: Check churn and lifetime GP 2 ways and require them to agree
hypothesis: If subscription LTV is computed both by the churn method and the cohort method and the 2 must agree, then a formula error in either method is caught before it drives a spending decision.

signal.check: Subscription LTV is reported from only 1 method with no cross-check against the other.

expected_effect.size: source case: both methods agreed at 92 dollars

prerequisites: Subscriber counts by period
Cohort survivorship data
steps: Compute churn = cancellations divided by prior-period subscriber base, stating the period.
Compute churn-method LTV = gross profit per order times orders per period divided by churn.
Compute cohort-method LTV by starting with 1,000 customers, applying survivorship each period, summing gross profit, and dividing by 1,000.
Require the 2 figures to agree within rounding before using either for a decision.
For non-subscription repeat customers, use the rolling 6-month return rate instead of churn.

test.method: Compute both LTV methods for the current subscriber base and check the gap between them.

title: Add discount cost together with CAC as 1 true cost of acquisition
hypothesis: If discount cost and media CAC are tracked as 1 combined true cost of acquisition, then a discount that lowers conversion cost is credited correctly instead of being booked as pure margin loss.

signal.check: Discount cost on first orders and CAC are reported and budgeted as 2 unrelated numbers.

expected_effect.size: holds only when CAC falls by the same dollar amount the discount cost; must be tested, not assumed

risk.note: Assumes a conversion lift from the discount; test it, do not assume it.

prerequisites: Discount cost on first orders tracked separately
steps: Compute true_cost_of_acquisition = discount cost per new order plus cac_media.
Track this combined figure against the CAC ceiling, not media CAC alone.
Test whether the discount actually lowers CAC by the same dollar amount before assuming it does.
Report the combined figure whenever a discount is used to drive new-customer acquisition.

test.method: A/B test the discount against a no-discount control and compare true cost of acquisition in each arm.
test.read_point: After the test reaches a decision-grade sample

title: Own discounts and marketing as 1 pool, and pick the split that maximizes total post-marketing CM
hypothesis: If discount depth and ad spend are decided together against total post-marketing CM at equal total spend, then the store picks the split that makes the most total profit instead of optimizing per-customer margin alone.

signal.check: Discount depth decisions are made separately from ad spend decisions, with no combined total-CM comparison.

expected_effect.size: source grid: 100,000 dollars spend with 0 discount gives 25,000 dollars post-marketing CM; 60 dollars off with a 3.8 percent conversion gives 63,000

risk.note: Conversion lift by discount level is an assumption until tested.

prerequisites: Conversion rate by discount level, even as a working assumption
Ad spend and blended CPC
steps: Model several discount levels at equal ad spend: sessions, purchases, CAC, net AOV, CM2 and CM3 per customer and in total.
Pick the scenario with the highest total CM3, not the best per-customer margin.
Mark conversion-rate-by-discount assumptions clearly and hand the riskiest ones to a test.
Assign 1 owner for the combined discount-and-media pool so decisions are not split across teams.

test.method: Run the discount vs CAC grid model, then A/B test the top 2 discount levels against each other.
test.read_point: After the test reaches a decision-grade sample

title: Recalculate break-even ROAS and CAC at the discounted price before any public discount
hypothesis: If break-even ROAS and CAC are recalculated at the discounted price before a discount goes public, then a discount that requires efficiency never seen on paid does not go live.

signal.check: A blanket discount is planned with no recalculated break-even ROAS or CAC at the discounted price.

expected_effect.size: source example: a 100 dollar price with 40 dollar margin has break-even ROAS 2.5; at 30 percent off with costs unchanged, break-even ROAS rises to 7

risk.note: Running an unaffordable discount publicly can lose money at scale before it is caught.

prerequisites: CM2 percent at full price and at the proposed discounted price
steps: Compute break-even ROAS and CAC at the full price.
Recompute both at the discounted price with costs unchanged.
If the required break-even has never been observed on paid media, do not run the discount publicly.
Get sign-off from whoever owns the CAC ceiling before launching any blanket discount.

test.method: Compare the discounted break-even ROAS against the best ROAS ever observed on paid before approving the launch.

title: Model percent-off, BOGO and gift-with-purchase through their real cost shapes before choosing one
hypothesis: If percent-off, BOGO and gift-with-purchase are each modeled through their real cost shape (revenue given away vs cost given away), then the store picks the promo type that fits its product cost instead of picking by habit.

signal.check: A promo type is chosen without modeling its effect on CM2 and CM3, or a low-cost product runs percent-off instead of BOGO.

expected_effect.size: source example: 50 percent off sitewide model showed CM falling from 84 to 29 dollars, a 4 dollar loss per customer at 20,000 orders

risk.note: A large sitewide discount can produce a real per-order loss at volume if not modeled first.

prerequisites: Product cost per unit and fulfillment cost per order for the promoted product
steps: Model percent-off: revenue falls, product cost stays the same, fees fall with revenue.
Model BOGO: revenue stays the same, product cost doubles, shipping and pick-and-pack rise a little.
Model gift-with-purchase: gift cost against the AOV lift it is expected to drive.
Confirm the second unit ships in the same box before recommending BOGO.
Multiply the per-order model by expected promo volume and compare total CM3 across shapes.

test.method: Measure actual incremental conversion for the chosen promo shape against the modeled assumption.

title: Model Black Friday and sitewide-sale cohorts as lower-retention customers from day 1
hypothesis: If Black Friday and sitewide-sale customers are expected to have below-average retention from the start, then the promo is priced to make money on the first order instead of assuming it will earn back its discount over time.

signal.check: A Black Friday or sitewide-sale plan assumes normal repeat behavior with no retention discount applied to that cohort.

expected_effect.size: unknown, sale-period cohorts are expected to be worth less over time than average cohorts

prerequisites: Historical repeat rate for prior Black Friday or sale cohorts, if available
steps: Require the Black Friday or sitewide-sale offer to make money on the first order alone.
If historical sale-cohort retention data exists, apply a discount to expected repeat revenue from that cohort.
Do not use blended repeat-rate assumptions for sale cohorts in the forecast.
Review the actual retention of the sale cohort after 90 days to update the assumption.

test.method: Compare the sale cohort's 90-day repeat rate to the store's average cohort.

title: Attach the deepest discounts to a loyalty or subscription on-ramp, not a flash sale
hypothesis: If the deepest discounts are reserved for a loyalty or subscription on-ramp instead of a flash sale, then the customers who take the biggest discount self-select into higher lifetime value instead of into one-time bargain hunting.

signal.check: The deepest available discount runs on a flash sale rather than being reserved for a loyalty or subscription sign-up.

expected_effect.size: unknown, flash-sale converters are expected to need a big discount to buy again while on-ramp joiners self-select into higher LTV

risk.note: Offer structure change; no live-ad risk.

prerequisites: A loyalty program or subscription on-ramp offer already exists or can be built
steps: Identify the deepest discount currently offered anywhere in the store.
Move it, or an equivalent, onto the loyalty or subscription sign-up flow.
Reserve flat discounts for grade C stock instead of using them as the primary acquisition offer.
Track repeat rate for customers acquired through the on-ramp vs the flash sale.

test.method: Compare 90-day and 365-day repeat rate between customers acquired via the on-ramp discount vs the flash sale.

title: Model any promo above a few percent of monthly revenue on the full cost stack before running it
hypothesis: If a promo above a few percent of monthly revenue is modeled through baseline conversion, CAC, AOV, product and fulfillment COGS, CM and CM minus CAC before it runs, then its true profit or loss is known ahead of time instead of discovered after the fact.
does_not_apply_when: The promo is a small, routine discount well under a few percent of monthly revenue

signal.check: A promo expected to be a meaningful share of monthly revenue has not been modeled on the full cost stack before launch.

expected_effect.size: unknown, prevents an unmodeled promo from producing a surprise loss

risk.note: Modeling step before a live promo; the promo itself carries its own risk.

prerequisites: CM2 build for the promoted product
Expected promo order volume
steps: Model the baseline: conversion rate, CAC, gross AOV, net AOV after refunds, product COGS, fulfillment COGS, CM, CM minus CAC, monthly orders.
Model the promo variant on the same lines.
Multiply both by expected promo volume to compare total dollars, not just per-order margin.
Only approve the promo if total CM3 at the expected volume beats the baseline.

test.method: Compare the modeled promo outcome to the actual result after the promo closes.

title: Never write a no-refunds-during-promo policy; check statutory return rights instead
hypothesis: If a promo never states no refunds or returns, and the store instead checks its statutory return rights, then the store avoids a policy that ignores consumer law.

signal.check: A promo plan includes language suspending refunds or returns during the sale period.

expected_effect.size: unknown

risk.note: Ignoring statutory return rights can create legal exposure; verify against the brand's market before use.

prerequisites: Statutory return and refund rights for the brand's country, verified with a web check or the accountant
steps: Remove any no-refunds or no-returns language from promo plans.
Confirm the store's standard return policy meets statutory minimums for its market.
Model the promo's refund allowance using the standard return rate instead of assuming 0 returns.
Verify statutory return rights whenever the store enters a new market.

test.method: Review the next 3 promo plans for any no-refunds language before launch.

title: Never model pre-order, BNPL or try-before-you-buy revenue without a cancellation and return rate
hypothesis: If pre-order, buy-now-pay-later and try-before-you-buy revenue always includes a cancellation and return rate, then reported revenue is not recognized before the order is actually fulfilled and kept.
does_not_apply_when: The store does not offer pre-orders, BNPL or try-before-you-buy

signal.check: Pre-order, BNPL or try-before-you-buy revenue is modeled or recognized with no cancellation or return rate applied.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects revenue recognized too early on offers with real cancellation risk

prerequisites: Cancellation and return history for the offer type, or a conservative estimate
steps: Identify every offer type in use that defers fulfillment: pre-order, BNPL, try-before-you-buy.
Estimate a cancellation and return rate for each, from history or a conservative placeholder.
Apply that rate before recognizing revenue in any forecast or report.
Update the rate once real data accumulates for the offer.

test.method: Compare forecast revenue with and without the cancellation and return rate applied.
test.read_point: Before launching any new deferred-fulfillment offer

title: Test whether a discount lifts conversion enough to pay for itself, instead of assuming it
hypothesis: If every discount's conversion lift is measured with a split test instead of assumed, then the store learns whether the discount is a cheaper way to buy customers or pure margin loss before committing budget to it.

signal.check: A discount's expected conversion lift is used in planning with no split test run to confirm it.

expected_effect.size: unknown, the test itself determines whether the lift is real

risk.note: A/B test with a defined stop point; test design lives in the conversion rate optimization track.

prerequisites: Enough traffic to reach a decision-grade sample for an A/B test
steps: Design a split test comparing the discount against a no-discount or smaller-discount control.
Hand the test design to the conversion rate optimization process.
Measure conversion rate and true cost of acquisition in both arms.
Only commit the discount to ongoing use if the test shows a real, decision-grade lift.

test.method: Run the A/B test to a pre-registered sample size or duration before deciding.

title: Carry unredeemed loyalty points as a liability and charge their cost to the redeeming order
hypothesis: If unredeemed loyalty or reward points sit on the balance sheet as a liability and their margin cost is charged to the redeeming order instead of to marketing, then CM2 is not silently understated by an unaccounted-for future discount.
does_not_apply_when: The store does not run a points or rewards program

signal.check: Loyalty or reward points issued are not tracked as a balance-sheet liability, or their redemption cost is booked to marketing.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects CM2 by charging point redemption cost to the right order instead of marketing

prerequisites: Points issued and redeemed tracked by the loyalty platform
steps: Set up a liability account for unredeemed points, valued at their expected redemption cost.
Reduce the liability and charge the redemption cost to the order's CM2 when points are used.
Stop booking point redemption cost to marketing spend.
Reconcile the liability balance against outstanding points periodically.

test.method: Compare CM2 for orders redeeming points before and after the reclassification.

title: Run a break-even go or no-go check for any discount before it becomes public
hypothesis: If every discount runs through a single break-even go or no-go check covering full-price and discounted break-even, promo shapes, the discount-vs-CAC grid and cannibalization, then no public discount launches without a documented profit answer.

signal.check: No standard procedure exists for checking a discount's break-even before launch; discounts are approved ad hoc.

expected_effect.size: unknown

risk.note: Process addition; catches losing discounts before launch.

prerequisites: CM2 percent at the offer price
Conversion assumptions by discount level
CPC and ad spend
steps: Compute break-even ROAS and CAC at full price.
Repeat at the discounted price with costs unchanged; reject if break-even jumps past anything ever seen on paid.
Model BOGO, bundle or gift-with-purchase alternatives and compare CM2 and CM3 per order at expected volume.
Run the discount-vs-CAC grid at equal spend across 3 discount levels and pick the highest total CM3 within brand limits.
For sitewide sales, add expected cannibalization of full-price buyers and lower sale-cohort retention.
Prefer a loyalty or subscription on-ramp for the deepest discount and never plan no returns during the promo.

test.method: Run the full checklist for the next 3 planned discounts and confirm each produces a documented go or no-go.

title: Price bottom-up from a net profit target, never by keystone or an arbitrary markup
hypothesis: If every new product and price review starts from the net profit target and works up through cost of delivery, CAC and allowances, then price stops being set by a markup that ignores fulfillment, marketing and elasticity.
does_not_apply_when: The product is a rare hero-SKU repricing where the waterfall does not change often

signal.check: Prices are set by cost times a fixed multiple (keystone or another markup) with no link to CAC, fulfillment or the net profit target.

expected_effect.size: source estimates about 40 percent of startups price by keystone, calling it probably the worst way

risk.note: A price change can affect conversion; check the market before publishing a new price.

prerequisites: Landed cost per unit
CAC estimate for comparable products
Return and discount allowance percent
steps: State the net profit target and OPEX percent to get the CM3 target percent.
Add CAC estimate, return and discount allowance, shipping and fulfillment, and landed cost.
Solve for price using the waterfall formula, checking the denominator stays positive.
Check the solved price against competitor prices before publishing it.

test.method: Compare the waterfall-derived price against the store's current keystone or markup price for the same product.
test.read_point: Every new product launch and price review

title: Solve the waterfall price and check it against the market before publishing
hypothesis: If price is solved from the waterfall formula and then checked against competitor prices, then the store knows before launch whether the price needed to hit its margin target is realistic or requires a premium story.

signal.check: A new product's price has not been solved from the waterfall formula and checked against the market.

expected_effect.size: source example inputs solve to 63.51 dollars at a 20 percent CM3 target

prerequisites: CM3 target percent
CAC estimate
Return and discount allowance
Shipping and fulfillment quote
Landed cost per unit
steps: Compute CM3 target percent from net target plus OPEX percent.
Gather CAC estimate, return and discount allowance percent, shipping and fulfillment quote, landed cost per unit.
Solve price = fixed costs per order divided by (1 minus CM3 target percent minus percent charges).
Check the solved price against competitor prices for the category.
After launch, re-run the waterfall with observed CAC, returns and fulfillment at 60 to 90 days.

test.method: Confirm the contribution at the solved price equals the target percent within rounding.
test.read_point: At launch, then re-checked 60 to 90 days after

title: Position as premium or drop the product when the waterfall price sits far above market
hypothesis: If a product whose waterfall price sits far above the market either gets a real premium story or does not launch, then the store avoids selling at a price the market will not pay just to hit an internal margin target.

signal.check: The waterfall-solved price for a new product is well above where competitors sell similar products, with no premium positioning planned.

expected_effect.size: source example: everyone selling at 30 to 40 dollars, required price well above that

risk.note: Dropping a planned product has a real opportunity cost; weigh it against a genuine premium angle.

prerequisites: Waterfall price solved
Competitor prices for the category
steps: Compare the solved waterfall price to competitor prices for the category.
If it sits far above market, identify whether a real premium story exists (no one else selling a premium version).
If no premium story exists, do not launch the product at that price and cost structure.
Revisit sourcing, packaging or positioning before trying again.

test.method: Track conversion rate for a premium-positioned launch against the category average.

title: Stress-test every price 60 to 90 days after launch with observed cost and return data
hypothesis: If price is re-checked 60 to 90 days after launch using observed CAC, return rate and fulfillment cost, then a margin that no longer covers CAC and overhead gets caught and repriced before it drags down the whole catalogue.

signal.check: A product's price has not been reviewed since launch, or observed CAC and return rate have not been checked against the original waterfall assumptions.

expected_effect.size: unknown

risk.note: Review step; any resulting reprice or discontinuation is a separate decision.

prerequisites: Observed CAC, return rate and fulfillment cost for the product since launch
steps: 60 to 90 days after launch, pull observed CAC, return rate and fulfillment cost for the product.
Re-run the waterfall with these observed figures instead of the launch assumptions.
If margin no longer covers CAC and an overhead share, decide to reprice, sell more, or discontinue.
Repeat this stress test at every material COGS change.

test.method: Compare launch-assumption margin against observed margin at the 60 to 90 day mark.
test.read_point: 60 to 90 days after launch, and at every COGS change

title: Price different SKUs, colors and sizes separately instead of 1 flat price
hypothesis: If SKUs, colors and sizes are priced with small tests instead of 1 flat catalogue price, then the store captures margin the flat price was leaving on the table.
does_not_apply_when: A single hero SKU with no meaningful variant range

signal.check: Every variant in a product line carries the exact same price with no price testing across variants.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source host found he could charge more on some variants with no velocity drop using a price-testing tool

risk.note: A price increase can reduce velocity on a given variant; test design belongs to conversion rate optimization.

prerequisites: A price-testing tool or a controlled way to vary price by variant
steps: List variants (SKU, color, size) currently priced identically within a product line.
Pick 1 to 3 variants to test a price change on, using a price-testing tool or a controlled rollout.
Measure velocity (units sold) alongside the new price.
Keep the price change only where margin rises without a meaningful velocity drop.

test.method: A/B or staged-rollout test of a price change on selected variants against the current flat price.
test.read_point: After the test reaches a decision-grade sample, per 09-CRO

title: Forecast new-customer revenue and returning revenue from separate inputs, never as 1 line
hypothesis: If new-customer revenue and returning revenue are each forecast from their own drivers (ad spend for new, calendar and cohort curve for returning), then the forecast reflects what actually drives each segment instead of 1 blended guess.

signal.check: The revenue forecast is built as 1 total line with no split between new-customer and returning-customer drivers.

expected_effect.size: source calls this the number one rule of DTC forecasting

prerequisites: Cohort table
At least 1 year of daily ad spend and new-customer revenue
Dated marketing calendar
steps: Forecast new-customer revenue from planned ad spend and the spend-vs-efficiency curve.
Forecast returning revenue from cohort size, repeat rate by age and the dated marketing calendar.
Never copy last year's month if it had a launch or promo this year does not.
Sum the 2 forecasts into the monthly plan, keeping each visible separately.

test.method: Compare actual results to the combined and to each individual forecast segment for 1 month.

title: Build the revenue forecast from the dated marketing calendar, not a finance extrapolation
hypothesis: If the forecast is built from named actions on the marketing calendar (a launch, a send, a promo, a PR hit) instead of a straight-line extrapolation, then a higher number always traces to a specific action, not a hope.

signal.check: A revenue plan shows spend up and CAC flat, or a higher target, with no named action that explains the increase.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: A dated marketing calendar with launches, promos, sends, seeding and PR
steps: Build the forecast off the dated marketing calendar, not last year's revenue line.
For every planned increase, name the specific action driving it.
When the owner wants a higher number, ask which action will be added and what effect it should have.
Reject a plan that shows spend up 50 percent with CAC held flat and no named action.

test.method: Audit the current plan for any revenue increase with no named calendar action attached.

title: Forecast returning revenue from cohort size times repeat rate, then apply seasonality and events
hypothesis: If returning revenue is forecast by summing cohort size times repeat rate by age times returning AOV, then adjusted for a 3-year seasonality factor and planned events, then the forecast tightens from a rough guess to the source's claimed 1 to 2 percent accuracy.

signal.check: Returning revenue is forecast as a flat growth rate off last year, with no cohort-based build or seasonality adjustment.

expected_effect.size: source claims about 10 percent accuracy from the cohort sum alone, 1 to 2 percent with seasonality and events added

risk.note: Forecast methodology; needs enough monthly history to build a cohort curve.

prerequisites: Monthly new-customer counts back to the first available data
At least 2 to 3 years of returning revenue by month for seasonality
steps: Sum cohort size times repeat rate by age times returning AOV across all live cohorts for the target month.
Compute a 3-year seasonality factor as the mean of each month's returning revenue over the annual mean.
Add planned events that differ from last year (launches, promos not repeated or newly added).
Track forecast accuracy against actuals to refine the seasonality factor over time.

test.method: Compare the cohort-based forecast to actual returning revenue for the next 3 months.

title: Fit new-customer revenue to a spend-vs-aMER curve, excluding sale days and days under minimum spend
hypothesis: If new-customer revenue is forecast by fitting aMER against daily spend on about 1 year of clean data, then the required spend to hit a target can be solved instead of assumed at flat efficiency.

signal.check: New-customer revenue is forecast at a flat aMER regardless of planned spend level, with no fitted curve.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: About 1 year of daily ad spend and new-customer revenue
steps: Pull about 1 year of daily spend and new-customer revenue, excluding sale days, BFCM and days under a realistic minimum spend.
Fit a log or linear curve of aMER against daily spend, whichever fits best.
Read expected aMER at the planned spend level and compute expected new-customer revenue.
Back-solve the spend required for a target revenue, and name the action that closes any remaining gap.

test.method: Compare forecast new-customer revenue at the planned spend level against actual results.

title: Regress a short or broken revenue history to the mean instead of trusting it outright
hypothesis: If a short or structurally broken history (like a spike year or a post-iOS14 shift) is regressed toward comparable brands' curves instead of extrapolated directly, then the forecast does not repeat a one-off anomaly as if it were the new normal.

signal.check: The forecast extrapolates from a short history, a known outlier year, or a period before a known structural break with no adjustment.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Comparable-brand curves for spend vs efficiency and repurchase, where available
steps: Identify any known structural break in the store's own history (2020 to 2021, iOS 14, a tariff shift).
Cut data before the break, or weight it down, when fitting the forecast.
Where the store's own history is thin, blend in comparable-brand curves.
Give the forecast as a range, not a single point, when history is short.

test.method: Compare a forecast built with the regression adjustment against one without it, against actual results.
test.read_point: Each forecast cycle until enough history accumulates

title: When the owner wants a higher forecast number, name the specific action that closes the gap
hypothesis: If a request for a higher forecast number is answered with the named action (a launch, a promo, a new channel, more spend at a stated efficiency) that would close the gap, then the plan stays grounded instead of becoming a generic stretch target.

signal.check: The owner or board asks for a higher revenue number than the model produces, and the plan is simply raised without naming what changes.

expected_effect.size: source example: board wants 50 million, model says 40 million; the answer names the event, product, channel or creative volume that adds the gap or accepts 40 million

prerequisites: The base-case forecast already built from cohort curves and spend curves
steps: When a higher number is requested, list what the base-case model already assumes.
Name the specific action (launch, promo, channel, spend level) needed to close the gap to the requested number.
State the added risk or cost of that action.
Let the owner choose the action or accept the base-case number, rather than raising the number with no plan behind it.

test.method: Track whether the next 3 forecast-gap discussions end with a named action or an unexplained higher number.

title: Do not plan on old category efficiency returning once competitor supply has grown
hypothesis: If a plan checks how much competitor supply has entered the category since an efficient period, then the plan stops assuming an old CAC or ROAS level will return on its own.

signal.check: A plan assumes acquisition efficiency will return to a level seen in an earlier, less competitive year, with no check on competitor entry since then.

expected_effect.size: source example: a supplement brand alone on its search term in 2022 competes against 50 listings now

prerequisites: A rough view of competitor count or listing growth in the category
steps: Check how many competitors have entered the category since the store's most efficient acquisition period.
If competitor supply has grown faster than demand, do not plan for the old efficiency to return.
Look for growth through new products, channels or stories instead of a hoped-for CAC recovery.
Revisit the category competition check yearly.

test.method: Compare the plan's assumed CAC or aMER against the category's current competitive density.

title: Set an annual budget separate from the rolling forecast and review budget-vs-actual on its own cadence
hypothesis: If the annual budget is kept separate from the rolling forecast, with its own budget-vs-actual review, then the board or owner sees both the original plan and the current reality instead of 1 number that keeps moving.
does_not_apply_when: The store has no board, investor or owner budget cycle to satisfy

signal.check: The annual budget and the rolling forecast are the same document, updated together, with no budget-vs-actual view.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: An approved annual budget
A rolling forecast process
steps: Lock the annual budget at the start of the fiscal year.
Keep the rolling forecast as a separate, regularly updated document.
Report budget-vs-actual on its own cadence (monthly or quarterly) alongside the rolling forecast.
Do not overwrite the original budget when the forecast changes.

test.method: Check that both the budget and rolling forecast are visible side by side in the next board or owner review.

title: Build the daily expected-revenue line from returning, new-customer and event forecasts combined
hypothesis: If the daily revenue expectation combines the returning-revenue forecast, the new-customer spend curve and named event effects, then the team can track actuals against a real daily line instead of only a monthly target.

signal.check: No daily expected-revenue line exists; the team only compares actuals to a monthly total at month end.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Cohort curve (P9)
1 year of daily spend and new-customer revenue
Dated marketing calendar
steps: Compute returning revenue by month from the cohort curve, seasonality and planned events.
Compute new-customer revenue by fitting aMER against planned daily spend, dropping sale days and days under minimum spend.
Overlay every past marketing action on revenue to estimate event effects, and add planned events for the period.
Add the email and SMS send calendar explicitly, since returning revenue rises on send days.
Sum into a daily expectation and track actuals against it, re-forecasting when observed CAC or aMER replaces a placeholder.

test.method: Check that new plus returning plus events ties to the monthly plan and every uplift has a named action.

title: Back-solve the OPEX line from the brand's own net profit target, not a universal percent
hypothesis: If OPEX percent is back-solved from the brand's own net profit target and OPEX plan instead of copying a universal 10 to 12 percent figure, then the target fits a brand with owned fulfillment or a large creative team instead of punishing it for a structure a lean Meta-first brand does not have.

signal.check: OPEX percent is being compared to a universal target like 10 to 12 percent with no back-solve from the brand's own net profit target.

expected_effect.size: source cites 10 to 12 percent as lean for a Meta-first US brand in 2025 to 2026, while a brand with owned fulfilment may sit higher and still be right to

prerequisites: Net profit target
CM3 target percent
steps: Compute CM3 target percent from the net profit target plus OPEX plan.
Back-solve the OPEX percent the business can afford at that CM3 level.
Flag OPEX above 15 percent and rising as a percent while revenue grows, without treating 10 to 12 percent as a mandatory target.
Get the owner's explicit agreement before using any external benchmark as a target.

test.method: Track OPEX percent against the back-solved target for 2 consecutive quarters.

title: Track fixed OPEX dollars per day and revenue per employee as scaling checks
hypothesis: If fixed OPEX dollars per day and revenue per employee are tracked as the business scales, then a lean team stays lean instead of OPEX creeping up unnoticed while output per person should be rising.

signal.check: Fixed OPEX dollars per day and revenue per employee are not tracked as separate metrics as the store scales.

expected_effect.size: source cites 1 million to 5 million dollars revenue per employee for lean AI-enabled brands

risk.note: Tracking only; treat as a planning lens, not a hard target.

prerequisites: Headcount and annual revenue tracked together
steps: Compute fixed OPEX dollars per day for the current period.
Compute revenue per employee (annual net revenue divided by FTE).
Track both metrics quarterly as the business scales.
Treat a rising fixed OPEX per day with flat revenue per employee as a flag to review headcount and tooling.

test.method: Track both metrics for 4 consecutive quarters and compare their trend to revenue growth.

title: Size full-time payroll at 12 percent of the lowest revenue month, cover peaks with flex labor
hypothesis: If full-time payroll is sized to 12 percent of the lowest revenue month, with flex labor covering peak demand, then the business does not carry a fixed payroll cost the slow season cannot support.
does_not_apply_when: The business has little revenue seasonality and no meaningful low month

signal.check: Full-time payroll is sized to a peak or average month, with no check against the lowest revenue month.

expected_effect.size: source example: a lowest month of 600,000 dollars gives a 72,000 dollar monthly payroll baseline

risk.note: Resizing payroll has real people implications; this rule skips legal, notice, quality and culture costs and needs judgment, not a mechanical cut.

prerequisites: Monthly revenue for the full year
Current payroll and on-costs
steps: Find the lowest revenue month of the year.
Compute the payroll baseline as 12 percent of that month's revenue.
Compare the baseline to current full-time payroll and on-costs.
Move any excess above the baseline to flex labor: agencies, freelancers, seasonal hires, offshore, or AI tools.

test.method: Compare OPEX percent before and after aligning payroll to the low-month baseline.

title: Build payroll in the store's own operating buckets plus on-costs, not a giant flat tab
hypothesis: If payroll is modeled in the store's real buckets (marketing and creative, warehouse and fulfilment, support, executive) plus on-costs, then the model matches how the store actually staffs for peak instead of a generic 700-row spreadsheet nobody uses.

signal.check: Payroll planning lives in an overcomplicated, generic spreadsheet with no bucket structure matching how the store staffs.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects a payroll model that does not match real staffing buckets

prerequisites: Headcount by role and salary
steps: Group headcount into buckets: marketing and creative, warehouse and fulfilment, support, executive.
Compute payroll per bucket as annual salary divided by 12 times headcount.
Add on-costs (about 25 percent in the US, swap in the country's real rate) per bucket.
Rebuild the model in these buckets instead of a long flat row-by-row tab.

test.method: Compare the bucketed model's total payroll to the actual payroll run for 1 month.

title: Delay heavy people spend and reinvest through marketing first
hypothesis: If heavy people spend is delayed until the business can attract and identify great hires, with reinvestment flowing to marketing first, then OPEX growth does not outpace the revenue it is meant to support.

signal.check: New headcount is being added ahead of a clear need or a proven ability to hire well, while marketing budget growth lags revenue growth.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source treats this as a delay, not a never-hire rule, since people are also the biggest lever and set the revenue ceiling

risk.note: Delaying a genuinely needed hire has its own cost; this is a timing judgment, not a permanent freeze.

prerequisites: OPEX and marketing spend trend by month
steps: Review planned new hires against whether the role is truly load-bearing right now.
Delay hires that are not clearly load-bearing until a strong candidate is identified.
Direct the freed budget toward marketing reinvestment first.
Revisit the delayed hires once the 7-figure brand stage the source flags is reached.

test.method: Track OPEX percent and marketing percent of revenue over the next 2 quarters.

title: Split ownership: 1 person on daily CM and ad pacing, 1 on the calendar and inventory plan months out
hypothesis: If 1 owner tracks daily CM3 and ad pacing while another owns the marketing calendar and inventory plan months out, then a stockout or a BFCM peak is not missed while someone is heads-down on today's spend.
does_not_apply_when: The team is a founder working alone with no one to split the role to

signal.check: The same person owns both daily spend decisions and the long-horizon marketing calendar and inventory plan, with no explicit split.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source claims daily CM tracking without a long-horizon owner drives short-term over-optimizing

prerequisites: A team of at least 2 people beyond the founder
steps: Assign 1 person to own daily contribution margin tracking and ad pacing decisions.
Assign a second person to own the marketing calendar and inventory plan months out.
Have the long-horizon owner flag any upcoming stockout risk or seasonal peak to the daily owner in advance.
Review the split quarterly to confirm both roles have the bandwidth they need.

test.method: Track whether any stockout or missed peak occurred in the quarter after the split, compared to before.

title: Check free cash flow every month, not just net income
hypothesis: If free cash flow is checked alongside net income every month, then a business that looks profitable on paper but is losing real cash gets caught before a big inventory buy, build or loan makes it worse.

signal.check: Only net income is reviewed at the monthly close, with no free cash flow figure computed.

expected_effect.size: source model: net income positive all 6 months, FCF positive in only 2

prerequisites: Monthly P&L, balance sheet and cash flow for at least 6 months
steps: Compute operating cash flow from net income plus depreciation and amortization, adjusted for working capital changes.
Subtract capex to get free cash flow.
Report net income and FCF side by side every month.
Investigate any month where they point in different directions before a big spend decision.

test.method: Track net income and FCF side by side for 3 consecutive months.
test.read_point: Every monthly close, and before any large inventory buy, build or loan

title: Report inventory value next to profit at every close so a cash-negative profitable month is caught
hypothesis: If inventory value on the balance sheet is reported next to profit at every close, then a brand that is profitable on paper but cash-negative because of unsold stock gets caught before the founder assumes the cash exists.

signal.check: Monthly close reports profit with no inventory balance shown alongside it.

expected_effect.size: source example: 2 million dollars profit, 3 million dollars of unsold inventory bought, cash down 1 million

prerequisites: Inventory value by SKU and date
steps: Pull the inventory balance at cost for the closing month.
Report it next to net profit and cash balance in the close pack.
Confirm there is a sell-through plan for any large inventory build.
Flag the month if profit and cash diverge without an explained inventory build.

test.method: Compare profit, inventory balance and cash balance for 3 consecutive months.

title: Add a cash line and a lowest-cash-month figure to every growth plan
hypothesis: If every growth plan carries a projected cash line and states the lowest cash month, then the store spots a liquidity problem before it dies of one, since many ecommerce businesses fail on cash, not unit economics.

signal.check: A growth plan projects revenue and profit with no cash line or lowest-cash-month figure.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source states many ecommerce businesses die of liquidity, not unit economics

prerequisites: Opening cash
Forecast orders
Landed costs, deposit and balance terms
OPEX and loan schedule
steps: Build the cash line into every growth plan alongside revenue and profit.
Find the lowest projected cash month and its dollar amount.
Start a raise or facility conversation early if the lowest point is tight, since raising takes time.
Reject any growth plan presented without a cash line.

test.method: Review the last 2 growth plans presented and confirm each carries a cash line and lowest-cash-month figure.

title: Trade margin for cash on purpose, in writing, when the owner says cash is the priority
hypothesis: If every deliberate cash-over-margin trade (liquidation, a discount, paying more for longer supplier terms) is written down with its P&L cost, then the store makes the trade knowingly instead of losing margin without tracking what it bought in cash.

signal.check: The owner has said cash is the current priority, but decisions that trade margin for cash are not being logged with their P&L cost.

expected_effect.size: unknown

risk.note: Documentation discipline; the underlying trade (liquidation, discount, terms) carries its own risk.

prerequisites: The owner has explicitly stated cash is the current constraint
steps: Confirm with the owner whether cash or margin is the current priority.
For every trade made to raise cash (liquidation, discount, paying more for longer terms), write down its expected P&L cost.
Track the actual cash raised against the logged cost.
Revert to margin-first decisions once the owner says the cash priority has passed.

test.method: Review the log of cash-for-margin trades at the end of the cash-priority period.
test.read_point: At the end of the stated cash-priority period

title: Read the 3 statements together and reconcile profit to free cash flow every month
hypothesis: If the P&L, balance sheet and cash flow statement are read together every month with the drivers of any profit-cash gap ranked by size, then a diverging month gets explained instead of dismissed.

signal.check: No monthly process reconciles net income to free cash flow using all 3 financial statements together.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Monthly P&L, balance sheet and cash flow for at least 6 months
steps: Compare revenue, net income, FCF and cash balance side by side and mark any month where net income and FCF diverge.
On the income statement, mark cash-equal lines (payroll, ads, rent, software) vs non-cash or mistimed lines (depreciation, product cost timing, tax accrual).
On the balance sheet, check assets equal liabilities plus equity and track movements in cash, inventory, receivables, payables and loans.
For each divergent month, rank the drivers by size: inventory build, capitalized development, tax payment, principal repayment.
Confirm a planned inventory build has a sell-through timeline; fix an unplanned one before it repeats.

test.method: Check that net cash flow ties to the bank balance and every divergent month has a named, ranked cause.

title: Build a rolling 13-week cash forecast and find the lowest cash point before it happens
hypothesis: If a rolling 13-week cash forecast tracks receipts, payroll, ad billing, PO payments, tax and loan dates by week, then the lowest cash point and any shortfall is known weeks ahead instead of discovered when a payment bounces.

signal.check: No rolling 13-week cash forecast exists, or cash planning only happens at the monthly level.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Opening cash
Forecast orders
Supplier deposit and balance terms
OPEX and loan schedule
Tax calendar
steps: Roll inventory forward with forecast units sold and arrivals lagged by lead time, ensuring no negative month.
Schedule PO cash at deposit and balance dates using weighted landed cost.
Build the mini monthly cash flow: opening cash plus net income minus inventory paid plus product COGS of units sold minus other capex minus principal minus tax paid.
Break the model into 13 weekly buckets: receipts by channel, payroll dates, ad billing, PO dates, tax dates, loan dates, rent.
Find the lowest cash point and reserve cash ahead of any known tax payment.

test.method: Check that closing cash of 1 month equals opening cash of the next, inventory never goes negative, and the 13-week and monthly views agree in the overlap.

title: Allow a spend increase during a cash squeeze only when all 5 clearance conditions hold
hypothesis: If a spend increase during a cash squeeze is only allowed when media demonstrably drives revenue, the stock is grade C or D, the spend is ring-fenced at a stated efficiency, success is judged on cash recovered, and the 13-week forecast can fund it, then a reflex spend cut or a reckless spend increase are both avoided.

signal.check: A cash squeeze is being handled by either a reflex spend cut or an unring-fenced spend increase, with no explicit check against the 5 conditions.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source frames a 40 percent reflex media cut as risking a revenue spiral

risk.note: Getting this decision wrong in either direction (cutting too hard or spending recklessly) can worsen the cash position.

prerequisites: Grade C and D stock identified
13-week cash forecast
aMER for the clearance funnel
steps: Confirm media demonstrably drives revenue: aMER on the clearance funnel is above break-even.
Confirm the stock being cleared is grade C or D, not core inventory.
Ring-fence the clearance spend in its own funnel line at break-even or a stated slight loss.
Judge success on cash recovered per week, not on ROAS.
Confirm the 13-week cash forecast can fund the spend until the cash returns.
If any condition fails, hold or cut spend instead of raising it.

test.method: Track cash recovered per week from the ring-fenced clearance funnel against the 13-week forecast.

title: Roll inventory forward with lead time before modeling cash, and never let it go negative
hypothesis: If inventory is rolled forward as prior stock minus forecast sales plus arrivals lagged by lead time, then a projected negative month (a stockout) is caught and the PO moved or enlarged before it happens.

signal.check: Cash planning does not include a rolled inventory forecast with lead time, or a projected stockout has not been checked before committing to a cash plan.

expected_effect.size: source models use 3 to 4 months lead time and a 4-month order cycle

risk.note: Planning step; the resulting PO decision carries its own cost.

prerequisites: Supplier lead time
Forecast units sold
Current inventory on hand and on order
steps: Roll inventory forward: prior period stock minus forecast units sold plus arrivals lagged by lead time.
Check every projected month for a negative balance.
If a month goes negative, move the PO earlier or enlarge it before committing the cash plan.
Size the next PO to cover lead time plus order cycle time, minus inventory on hand and on order.

test.method: Track actual inventory against the rolled forecast for 2 to 3 months and check no stockout occurred where the model showed cover.

title: Plan cash around the inventory investment (units times unit cost when paid), never per-unit COGS
hypothesis: If cash planning uses the inventory investment line (paid at deposit and balance dates) instead of per-unit COGS (recognized when sold), then the cash forecast matches when money actually leaves the bank.

signal.check: Cash forecasts use per-unit COGS timing instead of the actual supplier deposit and balance payment dates.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects a cash forecast that mistimes inventory payments

prerequisites: Supplier deposit and balance terms
steps: Get the deposit and balance payment dates and amounts for each open PO.
Build the cash forecast using these payment dates, not the COGS-recognition date.
Keep COGS on the P&L matching cost to the sale, separate from the cash timeline.
Update the cash forecast whenever a new PO is placed or terms change.

test.method: Compare the cash-basis forecast to actual bank movements for the next PO cycle.

title: Target days of inventory equal to supplier lead time per SKU, and grade stock A to D
hypothesis: If days of inventory per SKU is targeted to match supplier lead time, and stock is graded A to D by sell-through, then aged stock that ties up cash gets identified and worked instead of sitting unnoticed.

signal.check: Days of inventory per SKU is not tracked against lead time, or no SKU grading exists.

expected_effect.size: source examples of aged stock: 1,000 days in one case, 400 days after a failed launch in another

prerequisites: Units on hand and cost by SKU
Supplier lead time by SKU
Sell-through rate by SKU
steps: Compute days of inventory per SKU: units on hand divided by average daily units sold.
Compare against the SKU's supplier lead time.
Grade each SKU A to D by sell-through or days outstanding.
Route grade C and D stock to a liquidation review.

test.method: Track days of inventory for the top 20 SKUs monthly against their lead time.

title: Run a weekly inventory-and-media meeting to match spend to stock position
hypothesis: If a weekly meeting checks days of stock against lead time and against SKU-level ad spend, then a hero SKU never gets high-CAC ad spend right before it stocks out.

signal.check: No weekly process compares SKU-level days of stock against SKU-level ad spend.

expected_effect.size: source example: 30 days of stock against an 80-day reorder cycle should trigger raising the ROAS target sharply or pausing

prerequisites: Days of inventory by SKU
SKU-level ad spend
steps: Hold a weekly meeting with ops and whoever runs media.
Review days of stock vs lead time for the top-spending SKUs.
If a top SKU will sell out before restock, raise its ROAS target sharply or pause its ads.
Move spend to SKUs with stock, including aged stock that needs to move.

test.method: Track whether any hero SKU sold out while still carrying ad spend over the next quarter.

title: Score every purchase order on the marginal value of that batch, not just replenishment habit
hypothesis: If every PO is checked against whether the batch's marginal value justifies it, not just a reorder habit, then the business stops paying high CAC to sell stock about to run out and stops sitting on stock with no sales plan.

signal.check: POs are placed on a fixed reorder schedule with no check against current demand, stock position or a sales plan.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Days of stock and a sales plan per SKU
steps: Before placing a PO, check days of stock and whether spend is being used to sell it before it runs out.
Check whether stock already sitting has a plan to sell it.
Do not pay high CAC to move stock about to run out; slow spend instead if timing allows.
Do not order more of a SKU with no sales plan, even if it is the usual reorder cycle.

test.method: Review the next 5 POs for a documented marginal-value check before approval.

title: Write a demand plan with named channels and media dollars before any large PO
hypothesis: If every PO above a routine reorder starts with a written demand plan (units by channel, the media dollars needed, error bars for a new category), then the business does not order stock with no idea how it will be sold.

signal.check: A large PO is being placed with a revenue target but no unit-by-channel breakdown or media budget attached.

expected_effect.size: source failure case: a brand expected 20 million dollars from a new SKU with no idea of the media needed

risk.note: A large PO without a demand plan risks tying up significant cash in unsold stock.

prerequisites: CAC estimate for the category
Existing customer count for email and SMS
Influencer seeding plan, if any
steps: List expected units from existing customers (email and SMS), influencer seeding, and paid at a stated efficiency.
Compute media dollars for the paid share: units times CAC estimate divided by conversion to units.
Widen the error bars for a new category with no history.
Model PO timing against the cash cycle before ordering.
Get owner sign-off that the media budget exists before the PO is placed.

test.method: Compare actual sell-through against the demand plan's unit estimate after the PO lands.
test.read_point: After the new stock's expected sell-through window

title: Test demand with a small batch before committing to a large purchase order
hypothesis: If a new product launches with a small batch (about 100 units) run through ads to read real efficiency before a large PO, then the business does not commit big cash to a product with unproven demand.

signal.check: A new product is going straight to a large purchase order with no small-batch or pre-order demand test first.

expected_effect.size: source example: about 100 units live in 72 hours as a first test batch

risk.note: Small-batch cost is limited compared to the large PO it prevents.

prerequisites: A supplier able to fulfill a small first batch, or a low-MOQ supply chain
steps: List the new product on a small batch, about 100 units.
Run ads to it and read the efficiency (CAC, conversion) observed.
Use a fast, low-MOQ supply chain for this test batch and reserve a large-PO chain for proven items.
Use pre-orders when suppliers will not give flexible terms and demand already looks strong.
Only place the large PO once the test batch confirms demand.

test.method: Compare observed CAC and sell-through from the test batch against the assumptions used for the full PO.
test.read_point: After the test batch sells through

title: Run a liquidation funnel for aged stock instead of holding it to prop up the balance sheet
