hypothesis: If grade C and D stock runs through a dedicated liquidation funnel (unlisted page, ads excluding existing customers, judged on cash recovered) instead of sitting on the balance sheet, then the store frees cash for a better bet even when it does not strictly need the cash today.

signal.check: Stock graded C or D has been sitting for well beyond its lead time with no active liquidation plan.

expected_effect.size: liquidation efficiency runs at 1.0 or 0.8 ROAS vs 2.0 core, or break-even to a slight loss, per the sources

risk.note: Deep discounting can affect brand perception if not kept separate from the main storefront.

prerequisites: Grade C and D stock identified
steps: List SKUs with days outstanding far above lead time.
Build an unlisted product page or a whitelisted creator page, kept out of site navigation.
Run ads to it excluding existing customers, choosing either a deep discount or full price at a lower efficiency target.
Run other outlets in parallel: a narrative discount email if brand-safe, a bulk liquidator, or a new country.
Report cash recovered, not ROAS, and keep the spend in its own line so core aMER is not polluted.

test.method: Track days of inventory for the liquidated SKUs falling week over week, and total cash recovered.

title: Rotate dated goods nearest-expiry first and count stock periodically
hypothesis: If dated or seasonal goods ship nearest-expiry first, with logged stock movements and periodic counts, then waste and shrink get caught before they distort COGS assumptions or force a last-resort fire sale.
does_not_apply_when: The store carries no perishable, dated or seasonal goods

signal.check: No rotation rule exists for dated or seasonal stock, or stock counts do not happen on a regular schedule.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Expiry or season dates tracked per SKU batch
steps: Set a nearest-expiry-first rule for picking and fulfillment on dated or seasonal goods.
Log stock in and out consistently.
Count stock periodically and compare against the logs.
Investigate recurring count gaps as shrink or process error, and feed findings back into COGS assumptions.
Fire-sale stock only as a last resort, very close to expiry.

test.method: Track waste and shrink rate for 2 quarters after the rotation rule is adopted.

title: Rationalize SKU count at every product launch review
hypothesis: If every new launch names a SKU that leaves the catalogue, then a failed-launch pattern (30 to 40 percent sell-through then stall) does not keep parking cash on the balance sheet as the SKU count grows without limit.

signal.check: New SKUs are launched with no review of which existing SKU should be discontinued or reduced.

expected_effect.size: source claims many launches sell 30 to 40 percent of stock on the initial pop, then stall

risk.note: Review step; the actual discontinuation decision is separate.

prerequisites: Sell-through data by SKU
steps: At every launch review, name the SKU that will leave the catalogue as the new one lands.
Check sell-through history to identify the weakest current SKU.
Move the weak SKU into the liquidation funnel if it is aged.
Track total active SKU count over time to confirm it is not growing without limit.

test.method: Track SKU count and average days of inventory across the catalogue for 2 quarters after adopting the rule.

title: Manage the cash conversion cycle as the real growth cap, not ad efficiency
hypothesis: If the cash conversion cycle (days of inventory plus days sales outstanding minus days payable outstanding) is tracked and managed as the growth constraint, then a plan to grow faster than the CCC allows gets caught before it runs out of cash mid-stockout.

signal.check: A growth plan targets a revenue multiple with no check against the current cash conversion cycle and available self-funding.

expected_effect.size: source claims tripling an ecommerce business in a year is not realistic without multi-million self-funding, outside funding or financing

risk.note: Diagnostic step; the fix (financing, terms, deposit) carries its own risk.

prerequisites: Days of inventory, days sales outstanding and days payable outstanding
steps: Compute CCC = days of inventory plus days sales outstanding minus days payable outstanding.
Compare the growth rate implied by the plan against what the CCC and available cash can fund.
Flag any plan to grow faster than the CCC allows without new financing or terms.
Route a CCC squeeze into the CCC-fix procedure before approving faster growth.

test.method: Track CCC in days for 2 consecutive quarters against the growth plan's implied pace.

title: Fix a cash conversion cycle squeeze in order: smaller deposit, shorter lead time, longer terms, then financing
hypothesis: If a CCC squeeze is fixed in order (smaller deposit, shorter lead time, terms longer than production plus sell-through, then consignment, then financing), then the store negotiates its way out of the squeeze before turning to more expensive financing.

signal.check: Cash conversion cycle is tight and the store has gone straight to financing without first negotiating deposit, lead time or terms.

expected_effect.size: source examples: 20 percent deposit up front with the rest on shipment; terms of 120 days against a 90-day production time for a negative CCC

risk.note: Trading a higher unit cost or a bigger commitment for better terms has its own cost; weigh it against financing cost.

prerequisites: Supplier lead time, MOQ, deposit and payment terms per supplier
steps: Map lead time, MOQ, deposit and payment terms per supplier and compute the current CCC.
Negotiate a smaller deposit up front, balance on shipment.
Look for a shorter lead time supplier or process.
Ask for terms longer than production plus sell-through, trading a slightly higher unit cost, a longer contract, or a bigger commitment.
Move toward consignment over time where possible.
Only turn to financing after these options are exhausted, and stress-test it first.

test.method: Compute CCC before and after the negotiated changes.

title: Score every new product idea against 1 of 3 named problems: margin, volume or cash
hypothesis: If every new product idea is scored against margin, volume or cash as the named problem it solves, then product development spends effort on the lever the business actually needs instead of a merely interesting product.

signal.check: A new product idea is being pursued with no stated problem (margin, volume or cash) it is meant to solve.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: A clear read on the store's current constraint (margin, volume or cash)
steps: Identify the business's current constraint: thin margin, low volume, or cash tied up seasonally.
For every new product idea, name which of the 3 problems it is meant to solve.
Reject or deprioritize an idea with no named problem, however appealing the product.
Confirm after launch that the product actually moved the named metric.

test.method: Review the last 3 product launches for whether each had a named problem, and check whether it moved the metric.

title: Classify SKUs monthly as champion, hidden gem, growth driver or underperformer
hypothesis: If every SKU is classified monthly by volume, revenue, media spend and efficiency into champion, hidden gem, growth driver or underperformer, then spend and inventory decisions scale the right SKUs instead of treating the whole catalogue the same.

signal.check: No monthly SKU classification exists; spend and inventory decisions are made SKU by SKU with no shared framework.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: SKU-level spend, units, revenue and stock
steps: Pull volume, revenue, media spend and SKU-level efficiency for the month.
Classify each SKU: champion (strong on all), hidden gem (high volume, low spend), growth driver (spend and revenue both rising), underperformer (high inventory, low velocity).
Scale hidden gems and growth drivers with more spend where the CAC ceiling allows.
Turn underperformers to cash through the liquidation funnel.

test.method: Track how many SKUs move classification month over month and whether scaled SKUs actually grew.

title: Stress-test slower sales and lower efficiency before taking on financing
hypothesis: If any financing decision is stress-tested against slower sales and lower efficiency before signing, then the business does not borrow against an optimistic case that leaves net margin near 0 if growth slows.

signal.check: A financing decision (inventory loan, merchant cash advance, revenue-based financing) is being made off the base-case forecast with no downside stress test.

expected_effect.size: source has seen about 5 cases of spend 20K to 200K a month, revenue 2M to 7M, millions in inventory financing, net margin near 0

risk.note: Analysis step; the financing decision itself carries real risk if skipped.

prerequisites: Base-case P&L and cash forecast
Proposed financing terms
steps: Take the base-case forecast used to justify the financing.
Rebuild it with slower sales and lower marketing efficiency assumptions.
Check net margin and cash position under the stressed case.
Only proceed if net margin stays above the owner's floor in the stressed case.

test.method: Compare actual results 2 quarters after financing against the stressed-case projection.
test.read_point: Before signing, then reviewed quarterly after

title: Never sell permanent equity to fund a few months of inventory
hypothesis: If short-term working capital needs are funded with inventory or revenue-based financing instead of permanent equity, then the founder does not give up a lasting ownership stake to solve a temporary cash timing problem.

signal.check: A fundraise is being considered mainly to cover 3 months of inventory purchases, with no short-term financing alternative evaluated.

expected_effect.size: unknown

risk.note: Financing terms and eligibility should be checked with a current web check before deciding.

prerequisites: Current inventory financing or revenue-based financing options available in the brand's market
steps: Identify the real need behind the fundraise: is it short-term working capital or permanent growth capital.
If it is short-term working capital, evaluate inventory financing or revenue-based financing first.
Check current terms and eligibility for these products before assuming they are not available.
Reserve equity fundraising for permanent growth capital, not a recurring inventory cycle.

test.method: Compare the cost of the short-term financing option against the value of the equity that would otherwise be given up.

title: Compare real borrowing options against reference cost-of-capital rates before choosing who carries the float
hypothesis: If a PO or peak-season financing decision compares credit card float, merchant cash advance and supplier terms against their real cost of capital, then the cheapest source of float gets used instead of whichever option is easiest to access.

signal.check: A financing choice for a PO or peak-season buy is being made without comparing the real annualized cost of each option.

expected_effect.size: reference rates in the source: credit cards about 30 percent, merchant cash advance about 70 percent; supplier-subsidized capital can be cheaper

risk.note: Comparison step only; verify current rates before deciding.

prerequisites: Quotes or terms for each financing option under consideration
steps: List every real financing option for the upcoming PO or peak-season buy.
Get the actual rate or fee for each: credit card float, merchant cash advance, supplier terms.
Compare against the reference rates and check for supplier-subsidized capital, which can be cheaper.
Choose the lowest real cost of capital that fits the timing need.

test.method: Track the actual cost paid for the chosen financing option against the alternatives considered.

title: Model financing repayments as cash outflows, never delete the inventory row
hypothesis: If a financing model keeps inventory payments in the cash schedule and treats financing draws and repayments as separate inflows and outflows, then the model does not accidentally hide the real cost of the loan by deleting the underlying inventory cost.
does_not_apply_when: The store carries no inventory financing or PO loan

signal.check: A financing model replaces the inventory purchase line with a revenue-share repayment line instead of keeping both.

expected_effect.size: unknown, corrects a model that hides the real financing cost by deleting the inventory row

prerequisites: Financing terms and repayment schedule
steps: Keep the inventory payment line in the cash schedule as normal.
Add the financing draw as a separate cash inflow.
Add the repayment schedule as a separate cash outflow, never netted against the inventory row.
Check the model against the correct accounting treatment before using it for a decision.

test.method: Compare the corrected model's projected cash balance against the version that deleted the inventory row.

title: Model sales and spend separately from debt cost for any brand assumed to be using financing
hypothesis: If sales and marketing spend are modeled separately from debt cost, then interest expense does not distort the MER or aMER read for a 7-figure brand that is financing its inventory.

signal.check: MER or aMER appears to move when only the financing structure changed, with no separation between sales-and-spend and debt cost.

expected_effect.size: unknown, interest alone does not change MER

prerequisites: Interest and financing cost tracked separately from sales and marketing
steps: Assume any 7-figure client or brand may be using financing.
Keep MER and aMER calculations based only on sales and ad spend.
Report interest and principal separately, below EBITDA.
Re-check that a change in financing structure does not appear as a change in acquisition efficiency.

test.method: Confirm MER and aMER stay stable across a period where only the financing structure changed.
test.read_point: Every reporting period with active financing

title: Answer the next-$10,000 question by finding which channel returns the most incremental new-customer revenue
hypothesis: If the founder can answer where the next $10,000 in spend returns the most incremental new-customer revenue, and whether moving $10,000 between channels returns more, then budget allocation follows the marginal dollar instead of habit or gut feel.

signal.check: Budget changes are made without checking the marginal return of the next dollar in each channel.

expected_effect.size: unknown

risk.note: Analysis step; a +delta test or incrementality test is the reliable measure at scale.

prerequisites: Spend-vs-efficiency curve fit for each major channel
steps: For each channel, estimate the incremental new-customer revenue from an extra $10,000 in spend, using the fitted curve.
Push each channel until the marginal dollar's incremental aMER hits break-even.
Move $10,000 from the lowest marginal-return channel to the highest, while both stay above break-even.
Add tertiary channels only after the primary 3 channels hit the frontier.

test.method: Run a +delta test or incrementality test to confirm the modeled marginal return before moving significant budget.

title: Put spend where contribution per sale is highest, not where cost per acquisition is lowest
hypothesis: If budget is split by product-level contribution per sale instead of by lowest CPA, then spend stops flowing to the cheapest-to-acquire product even when it makes the least profit per sale.

signal.check: Campaign budget optimization is set to maximize conversions or lowest CPA with no check on contribution per sale by product.

expected_effect.size: source example: a hoodie made 24 dollars contribution at 45 dollars CPA vs a t-shirt's 12 dollars at 15 dollars CPA

risk.note: Reallocating budget away from the lowest-CPA product can look worse on a CPA report even while profit rises.

prerequisites: CM2 per order by product
CPA estimate by product's campaign
steps: Compute contribution per sale = CM2 per order minus the product's campaign CPA estimate for each product.
Rank products by contribution per sale, not by CPA.
Split campaigns by product economics rather than lumping them into 1 catch-all campaign.
For a low-CPA product that appears to sell without ads, cut its spend and validate with a holdout before assuming ads were driving it.

test.method: Run a holdout test on the low-CPA product's spend and compare sales with and without ads.

title: Compare every spend scenario on total CM3 at equal spend and on lowest cash month
hypothesis: If every spend scenario is compared on total post-marketing CM at equal spend and on its lowest projected cash month, instead of on revenue or per-customer margin alone, then the recommended scenario is the one that actually helps both profit and survival.

signal.check: A scenario answer (spend up 50 percent, move budget between channels, and so on) is compared on revenue growth or per-customer margin, with no total CM3 or cash comparison.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: The scenario answer procedure already built
steps: For each scenario, compute total CM3 (media and loaded) at the modeled spend level.
Compute the lowest projected cash month for each scenario.
Rank scenarios by total CM3 and by lowest cash month together, not by revenue or per-customer margin alone.
Show the rejected scenarios and why, next to the recommendation.

test.method: Review the last scenario decision and confirm it was made off total CM3 and lowest cash month.

title: Build a written scenario answer for spend changes with the marginal read and error bars shown
hypothesis: If every scenario question (spend up 50 percent, CAC plus 25 percent, moving $10,000) gets a written answer with expected aMER, CM totals, lowest cash month and a marginal read, then budget decisions are made from a documented model instead of intuition.

signal.check: A budget change is being discussed with no written scenario model covering aMER, CM totals, cash and the marginal read.

expected_effect.size: unknown

risk.note: Analysis deliverable; the underlying spend decision carries its own risk.

prerequisites: Spend-vs-aMER curve
Cohort table
13-week and monthly cash forecast
steps: State the question and the scenarios explicitly (for example plus $10,000 to Meta, to Google, spend plus 50 percent, CAC plus 25 percent).
For each scenario compute expected aMER, new customers, new-customer revenue, CM2, cm3_media and cm3_loaded totals, lowest cash month, LTGP:CAC 90-day and payback.
Run the marginal read per channel and stop where it hits break-even ROAS.
Where the curve is thin, say so and recommend a delta test or incrementality test.
Compare scenarios on total CM3 and lowest cash month, keeping the CAC line fixed unless the owner changes it.

test.method: Track actual results against the chosen scenario's projections for the following month.
test.read_point: Every scenario decision, reviewed the following month

title: Set the retargeting budget from existing-customer count and frequency, not a percent of spend
hypothesis: If the retargeting budget is sized from existing-customer count times target frequency times CPM, then it stops being an arbitrary percent of total spend and matches the audience actually being reached.

signal.check: The retargeting or existing-customer budget is set as a fixed percent of total ad spend rather than computed from audience size and frequency.

expected_effect.size: source example: 300,000 existing customers x 3 monthly frequency x 2.50 CPM / 1000 equals 2,250 dollars

prerequisites: Existing customer count
Existing-customer CPM from the platform's audience segment breakdown
steps: Count existing customers eligible for retargeting.
Set a target frequency of 3 to 6 times a month.
Get the existing-customer CPM from the platform's audience segment breakdown.

Compute budget = customers times frequency times CPM divided by 1,000, and sanity-check the result against the source's range (about 10,000 dollars up to 30,000 to 40,000 for brands with millions of customers).

test.method: Check the 7-day frequency on the platform after setting the budget; a reading above 8 signals overspending.

title: Never compare ROAS across platforms or move budget on a raw cross-platform ROAS gap
hypothesis: If ROAS is never compared across platforms, and budget moves are checked against a calibrated read instead of raw ROAS, then cutting a top-of-funnel channel on its ROAS number does not accidentally kill demand another platform was capturing.

signal.check: A budget move is being made because one platform's ROAS looks worse than another's, with no test design behind the comparison.

expected_effect.size: source pattern: TikTok drives impressions, Meta retargets, Google captures brand search; cutting TikTok on its own ROAS can kill top-of-funnel demand

risk.note: Cutting a channel based on a flawed comparison can reduce total revenue across the funnel.

prerequisites: Understanding of each platform's funnel role
steps: Map which stage of the funnel each platform primarily serves (top, middle, retargeting, brand capture).
Never compare raw ROAS numbers across platforms to decide a budget cut.
Route any cross-platform budget question to a test design (holdout or incrementality test) instead of a ROAS comparison.
Use platform ROAS only for directional reads inside that same platform.

test.method: Run a holdout test on the platform being considered for a cut before reducing its budget.

title: Calibrate platform ROAS with an incrementality factor before comparing to break-even
hypothesis: If platform-reported ROAS is multiplied by an incrementality factor from a real test before comparing to break-even ROAS, then a spend decision is not made off a platform number that overstates or understates the true incremental effect.

signal.check: Platform ROAS is compared directly to break-even with no incrementality factor applied, and no test exists to produce one.

expected_effect.size: example factor in the source: platform reads 1.0, a geo test reads 1.2, giving a factor of 1.2

risk.note: Incrementality tests carry their own cost and design considerations, held in 06-MEA.

prerequisites: An incrementality or geo-lift test result for the channel, from 06-MEA
steps: Pull the incrementality factor from the most recent test for the channel, if one exists.
Multiply platform-reported ROAS by the factor to get calibrated ROAS.
Compare calibrated ROAS, not raw platform ROAS, to break-even.
Optimize the platform setting on 7-day click without view-through, since it links most closely to new-customer revenue.
Where no test exists for a single-channel brand, check the daily correlation between 7-day-click ROAS and aMER as a substitute signal.

test.method: Check the daily correlation between 7-day-click ROAS and aMER; the source hopes for about 0.78 on a single-channel brand.
test.read_point: Whenever a new incrementality test completes, or monthly for the correlation check

title: Measure on 1 blended engine across channels once distribution widens beyond .com
hypothesis: If measurement covers 1 blended contribution across .com, Amazon and retail instead of separate P&Ls, then spend is not cut on .com just because a growing Amazon channel is pulling share from it.
does_not_apply_when: The store sells through only 1 channel

signal.check: The store measures .com performance in isolation while Amazon or retail sales are growing, and spend decisions are made off the .com-only view.

expected_effect.size: unknown, prevents a spend cut driven by channel-shift rather than a real demand drop

prerequisites: Sales data from every active channel (Shopify, Amazon, retail)
steps: Pull revenue and contribution from every active sales channel.
Build 1 blended contribution view across .com, Amazon and retail.
Before cutting .com spend because it looks weak, check whether Amazon or retail grew instead.
Report the blended view to whoever makes spend decisions, not a .com-only view.

test.method: Compare a spend decision made off the .com-only view against the same decision using the blended view.

title: Track FX exposure on multi-currency revenue separately from landed-cost FX
hypothesis: If FX exposure on multi-currency sales is tracked as its own line, separate from supplier-payment FX in landed cost, then a rate move between order and settlement has a named owner instead of silently hitting margin.
does_not_apply_when: The store prices and settles in only 1 currency

signal.check: The store prices or settles sales in more than 1 currency with no separate tracking of FX exposure on the revenue side.

expected_effect.size: unknown

risk.note: Verify against the accountant before deciding who absorbs rate moves.

prerequisites: Sales by currency
Order date vs settlement date for cross-border sales
steps: List every currency the store prices or settles sales in.
Track the gap between order-date rate and settlement-date rate for cross-border sales as its own line.
Name who absorbs a rate move (the brand, the customer, or a hedge) with the accountant's input.
Keep this separate from the supplier-payment FX already tracked inside landed cost.

test.method: Track cumulative FX gain or loss on the revenue side for 1 quarter.

title: Reconcile the 5 platform-to-books gaps every month with a named cause for each
hypothesis: If revenue, refunds, fees, spend and attribution are each reconciled between the platforms and the books every month with a named cause, then an unexplained gap gets caught instead of accepted as noise.

signal.check: No monthly process compares platform-reported numbers (Shopify, Meta, Google, Amazon, Metabase) against the accounting system with named causes for each gap.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Closed month in the accounting system
Platform exports for the same dates and timezone
steps: Compare platform gross sales, discounts, refunds processed, shipping collected and tax against books net revenue; name the gap cause (tax, timezone, accrual vs processed, shipping coding, currency).
Compare accrued vs processed refunds and post the true-up.
Compare platform-reported fees against fees booked in the books.
Compare platform ad spend against marketing booked in the books, naming any billing lag or credit.
Compare the sum of platform-attributed revenue against actual revenue and report it as a ratio, never as an error.
Compare units sold times landed cost against COGS posted; send any unexplained gap to the alert list.

test.method: Check that net revenue in the ladder equals books net revenue after named adjustments, with no unexplained gap above 1 percent of net revenue.

title: Publish a monthly bridge table between statutory COGS and internal cost of delivery
hypothesis: If a bridge table shows exactly which lines separate statutory COGS from internal cost of delivery every month, then the accountant's books and the marketing decision stay reconciled instead of drifting into 2 unrelated stories.

signal.check: Statutory COGS and internal cost of delivery are each reported, but no bridge table shows how they connect.

expected_effect.size: unknown

prerequisites: Statutory COGS and internal COD both computed
steps: List every line that internal COD adds beyond statutory COGS (outbound shipping, pick and pack, fees, warehouse staff).
Build a bridge table showing statutory COGS, each added line, and the resulting internal COD.
Publish the bridge table as part of the monthly close pack.
Use it to answer, in 1 place, why the 2 views differ for any given month.

test.method: Check that the bridge table's ending internal COD figure matches the CM2 build for the same month.
